title: Common Course Runtimes
text: Common Course Runtimes Category : Staff Use Only > Supplemental Material Date : 2026-05-18 05:34 Link : https://edstem.org/us/courses/98593/discussion/8077881 Pinned : True | Votes : 11 | Views : 1866 Post When performing runtime analysis for this course, we expect the analysis to be presented as the worst-case runtime analysis, presented in fully simplified Big-O notation. For example, O(2n + 3n) is expected to be presented as O(n) . As most assessable material for this course is written, this post exists to present the runtimes associated with common actions you may describe in your algorithms. When no supporting details are presented for special handling in a submission, the default action ( underlined ) and associated runtimes will prevail. For the runtimes presented below, n represents the length or size of the object being used. List In the context of the course, we will treat lists as standard arrays, indexable by integers starting at 1. Creating a list (empty) O(1) Creating a list with initial contents O(n) Adding an item to a list (appends to the end) O(1) Adding an item to a specific non-tail location of a list O(n) Remove an item from a list (swap tail element and pop) O(1) Remove an item from the list while maintaining order O(n) Check the length of a list (via counting) O(n) Check if a list contains an element (via scanning) O(n) Hash Table / Hash Set / Map / Set While common and practical for software development, these data types have worst-case performance that generally makes them undesirable. Unless the problem gives you data in this format (typically as a set ), you are unlikely to need this. Creating a hash table (empty) O(1) Creating a hash table with initial contents O(n^2) Adding an item to a hash table O(n) Remove an item from a hash table O(n) Check the length of a hash table (via counting) O(n) Check if a hash table contains an element (via scanning) O(n) Graph In this course, we will always treat graphs as adjacency lists, with an indexable list of vertices each pointing to a linked list of adjacent vertices. You can assume you know n (number of vertices |V|) and m (number of edges |E|). Traversing a graph O(n+m) (Includes reversing, copying, subgraphing, or anything that requires working with all vertices and edges in a graph) Operating on a single vertex v O(1) (Includes find, read, removal) Operating on all (or a subset of) vertices V O(n) (Includes find, read, removal) Operating on a single edge e=(u,v) O(n) This is due to the need to traverse up to n vertices in the adjacency list for vertex u , to find and operate on adjacency v . (Includes find, read, removal) Operating on all edges |E| O(n+m) (Includes find, read, removal) Accessing properties of an edge or vertex O(1) This assumes you already have access to the vertex or edge itself - that is, you have paid the runtime costs above for finding that vertex/edge, (e.g. weight, color, cost, capacity, etc.) Special note about simplifications If you KNOW something about the connectivity of the graph (e.g. MST, Flow, or the problem states it), it is possible to simplify some runtimes: We know the graph is connected and m >= n-1 O(n+m) = O(m+m) = O(2m) = O(m) We know the graph is a clique and m = n(n-1)/2 O(n+m) = O(n+n^2) = O(n^2) Responses (4) Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-05-19 15:58 (Votes: 0) Hi, I was wondering if "remove an item" refers to an index in the List section, and "remove an item" refers to a value in the Hash Table section? For the list, I couldn't see how you would get O(1) removal without first knowing where the item is. For the hash table (assuming chaining), I'm guessing that with the worst possible hash function (100% collisions), you would need an O(n) scan of the collided bucket to find the item to remove. Comment by User 137215 on 2026-05-19 16:21 (Votes: 1) For the list, I couldn't see how you would get O(1) removal without first knowing where the item is. The operation assumes you have some index i you want to remove. Of course if you have to "find" that index i , that will first take O(n) which is what the post above says: Check if a list contains an element (via scanning) * O(n) Once you have i and you have n , then you can do what it says and we will consider it O(1) . It is important to note that if you care about maintaining the remaining relative order, then you don't get this speedup. Comment by User 1015969 on 2026-05-20 13:21 (Votes: 0) Can you explain what "maintaining the remaining relative order" means? If you remove an element, the remaining elements in my mind still maintain their order. Ex. 1, 2, 3, 4 -> Remove 2 -> 1, 3, 4. The "order" is still ascending, or in other cases the "order" is the same minus a single element, but the river still flows Comment by User 215685 on 2026-05-20 23:20 (Votes: 0) you have to shift the other elements to not have the removed element there which is why removal is O(n) for arrays and O(1) for linked lists (assuming you have the pointer already). In practice some people will put a tombstone value for removals and won't have to shift all the other elements, but most often that's not the case. Comment by User 137215 on 2026-05-21 09:08 (Votes: 0) In practice some people will put a tombstone value for removals This can be a clever way for keeping order and performing removals. Unfortunately, the most common use of this is students picking a tombstone value that is also a valid input value... Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-05-21 04:39 (Votes: 0) want to remove the 2 1,2,3,4 step 1: swap with last 1,4,3,2 step 2: pop the tail element 1,4,3 congratulations, you have done an O(1) removal (but you decided to not care about relative order) Comment by User 649126 on 2026-05-22 07:47 (Votes: 1) Accessing T(n) in a 1-d list, let T(i), where 1<=i<=n, which is treated as an array we assume it takes O(1) and not O(n), right? Similarly, for 2-d lists, let T(i,j) for 1<=i, j <=n (treated as 2-d arrays) T(1,n) is extracted in O(1) and not O(n), correct? Thanks Comment by User 137215 on 2026-05-22 08:19 (Votes: 0) The DP tables follow the list runtimes above. If you go from 1D to 2D ( n x n ), then it goes from O(n) to O(n^2) and O(1) to O(1) for their respective operations. Comment by User 649126 on 2026-05-23 00:52 (Votes: 0) To summarize, Building/Creating a 1-D T(i) vector with 1<=i<=n takes 𝒪 (n) Building/Creating a 2-D T(i,j) table with 1<=i<=n and 1<=j<=n takes 𝒪 ( n 2 ) Accessing the i-th element of an 1-D T(i) vector with 1<=i<=n takes 𝒪 (1) Accessing the (i-th, j-th) element a 2-D T(i,j) table with 1<=i<=n and 1<=j<=n takes 𝒪 (1) Comment by User 281747 on 2026-05-22 11:43 (Votes: 0) Can we have this and the list of black box runtimes as reference on the exams? Comment by User 137215 on 2026-05-22 12:09 (Votes: 0) The problems on the exam will be presented similarly to how the problems are presented to you on the homework. Historically, the information you're asking for is not part of the exam 1 experience. Comment by User 281747 on 2026-05-23 09:38 (Votes: 1) Just curious why that is the case that there isn't a simple "note-card" provided for runtimes and blackbox functions and such? State licensing exams for traditional engineering like mechanical, electrical, civil, etc. all provide an equation sheet that's nearly 500 pages long. I imagine the goal of this course is to prove that we can apply our knowledge of these algorithms to unique problems rather than memorizing little details that can easily be referenced in real life. Comment by User 137215 on 2026-05-23 09:40 (Votes: 0) Just curious why that is the case that there isn't a simple "note-card" provided for runtimes and blackbox functions and such? The first half of the information is prerequisite knowledge students are expected to have prior to coming into the course. The ability to demonstrate that through the analysis of algorithms is being assessed. The second half is that there are a trivially few number of black boxes for exam 1, so knowing what they are, how to work them, and all those trivial details is part of what is being assessed. For future exams, when the number of black boxes are more, their names will likely be provided on the exam (at least, they have been historically). Comment by User 1015969 on 2026-06-20 13:00 (Votes: 0) For this item: __Operating on a single edge __ __e=(u,v)__ O(n) This is due to the need to traverse up to n vertices in the adjacency list for vertex u , to find and operate on adjacency v . I guess silly question; can we not use the same method mentioned here to find v in the adjacency list of u : Vertices are assumed to be labeled in such a way where they can be found by indexing into the array. Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-20 23:45 (Votes: 0) You cannot. Finding u takes O(1) , but finding where v is under u is what takes the time. The adjacency list is a list of linked lists , and the endpoints of the edges are stored in the linked list portion, which requires traversal to discover what it contains. For a general graph, any given vertex may have at most n-1 edges in its linked list, giving us the worst case runtime for a single edge of O(n) listed above.

title: Dynamic Programming Guidance
text: Dynamic Programming Guidance Category : Staff Use Only > Supplemental Material Date : 2026-05-18 06:07 Link : https://edstem.org/us/courses/98593/discussion/8077940 Pinned : False | Votes : 12 | Views : 4939 Post Solutions for Dynamic Programming (DP) Homework are in a written format with required components. This post is intended to give a general overview of those parts of such a solution. You will also see quiz and exam questions based on what constitutes a complete solution for DP. General Rules Submissions must be a Dynamic Programming approach to be eligible for points. No recursion or memoization. Inputs are always indexed starting from 1, unless stated otherwise (i.e. A[0] is usually invalid). Inputs may not be modified - they are to be treated as immutable. Tables may start from anywhere. If you need T[0] or T[-1] for a base case, this is valid as long as it is defined. Tables may only store primitive values: integers, decimals, characters, or Booleans. Required Sections (a) Subproblem Definition ALWAYS build on a subset of the input (e.g., A[1..i] ). Conceptually, the subproblem should always be defined against "previous" subproblems and not on the entire input. Is represented using words: " T(i,j) is the ....." Should use words from the problem statement without redefining their meaning May or may not require inclusion of the last element: ", including A[i] " The lectures use the phrase "which includes a[i] " to add the constraint "element a[i] must be used in the subproblem output." The phrases "which includes i " and "ending at a[i] " would also imply this constraint. These are not referring to the range of indices considered for the subproblem, 1,2,...,i , which is assumed inclusive [1, i ] . (b) Recurrence Definition #10 #10 #10 Read, absorb, and love #10 #10 #10 Expressed using mathematical notation - no programming constructs and not in words The table gets a single mathematical definition for all entries - there is no logic/flow control structure other than stating a set of conditional definitions. Defines the value of all table entries recursively to smaller subproblems Any referenced table entry must also be well-defined i.e. a reference for T(i-2) for 1 <= i <= n requires a definition for T(-1) It cannot be defined self-referentially (e.g. T(i) = max(T(i), ...) ) When base case(s) are necessary, include them and their applicable bounds Example: T(i,0) = 0 for 1 <= i <= n Always provide bounds for any variables used, scoped to where they are used Focus on table definitions, not a final solution (i.e. no return value) (c) Implementation Analysis (1,2,3,4) These parts should be based on the recurrence you use in the previous section. (1) State the number of subproblems in big-O notation This scales similar to runtime complexity A one-dimensional table ranging from indices -1 to n would be O(n) . e.g. O(n) , O(n*m) (2) State the runtime to fill this table Always, always in this course - worst case Big-O notation. e.g. O(n^2) (3) State how/where the final return is extracted from that table e.g. sum{T(*)} , max{T(*)} , T(n) , max(T(n), T(n-1)) (4) State the runtime to extract the final return in big-O notation Tips and Tricks You will be tempted to start with code. This is a terrible idea. Starting with code ensures your recurrence will be nearly impossible to craft. Do these sections in order - Dr. Vigoda does the same thing, and you should see how seamlessly the final solution comes together. Define a subproblem, which can then be translated to the mathematical recurrence, and the analysis can be easily derived from that. The lectures contain multiple approaches (LIS, LCS, Knapsack, CMM, etc.). When solving a new problem, first try to think of which approach makes the most sense to adapt for a solution to the new problem. Example Solution Expand the spoiler below for an example of what a complete DP solution looks like: Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) a. Define the entries of your table in words. E.g., T(i) or T(i, j) is ... Let T(i) = length of LIS in a[1...i] which includes a[i] b. State recurrence for entries of your table in terms of smaller subproblems. T(1) = 1 T(i) = 1 + max{T(j) if a[i] > a[j] : where 1 <= j <= i-1} where 2 <= i <= n c. Implementation Analysis (1) State the number of subproblems: O(n) (2) State the runtime for table fill: O(n^2) (3) State how the return is extracted: return max{T(*)} (4) State the runtime of that return extraction: O(n) Please use this thread to ask any follow-up questions regarding what constitutes a complete DP solution, or clarifications on the above information. Responses (12) Comment by User 0 on 2026-05-19 00:53 (Votes: 0) On exams, will the required formats for solutions to various types of problems be written down, or is the expectation that students memorize the solution templates for each type of problem? Comment by User 99740 on 2026-05-19 00:56 (Votes: 2) The Homework questions throughout the semester are formatted in the same way you'll see on the exam itself. So, in this case you'll get the main categories of things required, but of course not this entire post. Comment by User 649126 on 2026-05-19 09:23 (Votes: 1) Hi - My intention is not to get into the weeds but I am trying to understand why correctness (and exhaustiveness) do(es) not have to be proved in this course. Is it because a properly formulated and correct recurring relation guarantees correctness and exhaustiveness? IF we had to prove those two separately (for personal fun), are there 2 ways to prove correctness & exhaustiveness (either proof by induction assuming the optimal solution or by proving that the problem formulation can be seen as an acyclic DAG)? Also, in some problems we may be able to avoid storing the entire T[i] table in memory by storing a prev pointer. Should we always aim for best space complexity in our algorithms? For c (2) and c (4) - do we need a pseudocode block to justify our answer or for DP problems the pseudocode block is not required? Thanks, Alex Comment by User 137215 on 2026-05-19 10:43 (Votes: 0) Should we always aim for best space complexity in our algorithms? A noble goal, but not a factor your submission will be assessed on, unless the space itself causes a runtime issue. For c (2) and c (4) - do we need a pseudocode block to justify our answer or for DP problems the pseudocode block is not required? What does the embedded example solution in the post suggest? Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-05-23 14:52 (Votes: 0) The example suggests that no pseudocode is required for HW solutions nor for exam solutions. Comment by User 137215 on 2026-05-23 15:01 (Votes: 0) One mystery solved, one mystery remains. Comment by User 1312670 on 2026-05-19 21:05 (Votes: 0) SPOILER ALERT--this is about your solution in this line: T(1) = 1 T(i) = 1 + max{T(j) if a[i] > a[j] : where 1 <= j <= i-1} where 2 <= i <= n Don't you also need to cover the case where there is no such j? i.e. if there exists j, 1<=j<=i-1, s.t. a(j)<a(i)... otherwise T(i)=1 Comment by User 135758 on 2026-05-19 23:10 (Votes: 1) This is discussed in Course Readiness: https://edstem.org/us/courses/98593/lessons/171116/slides/988492 Dr. Vigoda is taking advantage of null set evaluation to assume max{} would evaluate to 0 in those cases. We can definitely make this more explicit: T(i) = 1 + max{T(j)} if a[i] > a[j] = 1 otherwise 1 <= j < i <= n Comment by User 971631 on 2026-05-21 06:39 (Votes: 0) Should the otherwise be 1 ? In the explicit branch it'd be 1 + max{} = 1 + 0 = 1 , since T(i) includes a[i] so the minimum is the lone element. Does the +1 carry into the otherwise too? Comment by User 135758 on 2026-05-21 06:44 (Votes: 1) Yes, fixed! Thank you for the correction. Comment by User 0 on 2026-05-22 06:15 (Votes: 1) Hey Tim - just to check, on exams are we also allowed to use null set evaluation (i.e. assume that the maximum of an empty set is equal to 0) or do we have to be explicit by defining something piecewise or using unions with a singleton set containing 0? I saw in your walkthrough for 6.3 you also use null set evaluation. Comment by User 137215 on 2026-05-22 07:00 (Votes: 1) This is the expected behavior . You do not need to call it out or do anything special. Comment by User 137215 on 2026-05-19 23:39 (Votes: 0) SPOILER ALERT--this is about your solution You can use This little guy if you want to make your spoiler less spoiler-y. Comment by User 0 on 2026-05-22 05:41 (Votes: 1) Question: For problems that require us to output a sequence or string (rather than just the cost or value of the sequence), are we allowed to use additional tables that we also fill using a dynamic programming approach or may we only define a single table containing primitive values and then extract the sequence using that table? E.g. for 6.2 Tim's solution uses the T table to backtrack and output the sequence of hotels but it's also possible to define some table H where H[i] gives the previous hotel in the optimal sequence. Comment by User 137215 on 2026-05-22 06:05 (Votes: 6) are we allowed to use additional tables that we also fill using a dynamic programming approach You are not limited to a single table, nor are you limited to only 1D, 2D, or 3D tables. With that said, commonly when attempting to solve a problem, if you believe you need multiple tables, or if you think you need more dimensions, you may want to consider whether something about the problem that would allow a simplification has been missed. Additionally, any secondary/helper table is constrained to the same storage limitations as the primary table. Which is to say, you can't "use a second table" and start filling it with tuples or other non-primitive data. For (c3) "State how the return is extracted", if you need to extract a solution instead of returning a single value, you can describe it in a few sentences - it does not need to be in the limited math notation that the recurrence itself requires. Comment by User 137657 on 2026-05-24 08:15 (Votes: 1) Is this a valid answer for 6.7 ? Specifically: Are we allowed to create modified copies of the input such as creating a reversed copy of the input sequence x? Are we allowed to **redefine the problem **as "the length of the longest common subsequence" if the original problem states finding the " longest palindromic subsequence"? Subproblem Definiton: Let y = the reversed sequence of x Let T(i,j) = the length of the longest common subsequence between x[1...i] and y[1...j] Base Case: T(0,j) = 0 for 0<=j<=n T(i,0) = 0 for 0<=i<=n Recurrence: T(i,j) = T(i-1,j-1) + 1 if x[i] == y[j]; where 1<=j<=n T(i,j) = max{T(i-1,j),T(i,j-1)} if x[i] != y[j]; where 1<=j<=n where 1<=i<=n Number of Subproblems = O(n^2) Time to fill = O(n^2) Extract answer : Return T(n,n) Time to return O(1) Comment by User 135758 on 2026-05-24 08:22 (Votes: 3) (ENDORSED) This would be acceptable if there is a proper mathematical definition for y . Specifically: y i = x n − i + 1 for 1 ≤ i ≤ n Comment by User 665931 on 2026-06-09 05:49 (Votes: 0) Where would something like this be stated in solution format? To me it makes just as much logical sense to state in Part 1 that we are "reversing and storing the input sequence" and aware that this is +O(n) time-wise, but saying it must be stated mathematically makes me think it would be couched in part two (which significantly changes the face of this part vs. other more standard problems). Can you give a rough estimate of how much would be deducted in the exam for stating only in words? Comment by User 135758 on 2026-06-09 05:50 (Votes: 1) This type of structure should be stated as part of the general recurrence. This is true for any type of helper function or auxiliary table used in the recurrence. Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-05-25 04:47 (Votes: 0) In the "define subproblem in words" section, do we need to specify bounds of indices? Comment by User 135758 on 2026-05-25 04:49 (Votes: 3) We typically don't recommend including bounds in the Subproblem Definition. The reason is revealed in the lectures: sometimes Dr. Vigoda includes bounds relevant for the *table *that otherwise would be invalid for the range of the inputs. This is explicitly resolved in a complete recurrence relation so we recommend omitting the bounds in the Subproblem Definition. Comment by User 495006 on 2026-05-25 18:02 (Votes: 0) In the case that the result is a list, for example, the items used in a knapsack problem, how do we write it without using pseudo code? Could you give us an example? Comment by User 137215 on 2026-05-25 22:51 (Votes: 0) https://edstem.org/us/courses/98593/discussion/8077940?comment=18704036 https://edstem.org/us/courses/98593/discussion/8079608?comment=18709407 Comment by User 488161 on 2026-05-28 23:38 (Votes: 0) Just for clarification, in the Recurrence Definition section, would it be acceptable to explicitly break it into the following subsections? (b) Recurrence Definition: ** ** 1. The base case: (e.g. T(0) = 0) ** 2. The general case: T(i) = ...** ** 3. The Bounds: 1 <= i <= n** Just wanted to check as following this format helps me to ensure that I am addressing all of the necessary parts of the recurrence. Comment by User 135758 on 2026-05-29 00:29 (Votes: 0) yes. This is totally fine. Comment by User 488161 on 2026-05-29 00:36 (Votes: 0) Thanks, appreciate it. Comment by User 137215 on 2026-05-29 01:27 (Votes: 0) To add some clarification, since "The Bounds" feels awfully ominous: If both the base case(s) and the general recurrence need bounds, they both need their own set of bounds, even if they are the same Which is to say: The Base Case: T(i, 0) = 0 The General Case: T(i, j) = T(i-1, j-1) + 1 The Bounds: 1 <= i <= n, 1 <= j <= n Is problematic. Even replacing The Bounds: 0 <= i <= n, 1 <= i <= n, 1 <= j <= n remains problematic, as graders are not going to map the correct bounds to parts of your recurrence for you. It would appear your 3 part structure can work without ambiguity for constant-time base cases though. With the trade-off being that you've now got to determine how you want to handle the two different variants while practicing. Comment by User 488161 on 2026-05-29 01:44 (Votes: 0) That makes sense, and is something I wasn't certain about. Do you feel it would be better from a graders perspective to have the bounds included in the general case (e.g. T(i,j) = T(i-1, j-1) + 1, where 1 <= i <=n and 1 <= j <=n)? Comment by User 137215 on 2026-05-29 02:01 (Votes: 0) Yes. In the example above, the clearest / most common way would be: T(i, 0) = 0, for 0 <= i <= n for 1 <= i <= n, 1 <= j <= n T(i, j) = 1 + T(i-1, j-1) Or you can put it at the bottom: T(i, 0) = 0 where 0 <= i <= n T(i, j) = 1 + T(i-1, j-1) where 1 <= i <= n, 1 <= j <= n Or you can use where and put it at the top. Or you can exclude for/where honorariums and just have the bounds colocated. Making it as easy as possible for the grader to see which bounds belong to which parts improves first-pass grading accuracy (when the bounds are correct or even when they are incorrect) and avoids sadness (when the bounds might be correct, but are ambiguous or incomplete). Comment by User 488161 on 2026-05-29 03:15 (Votes: 0) I'll make sure to use this format moving forward. Thanks, I appreciate it. Comment by User 1664716 on 2026-05-29 16:47 (Votes: 0) From the perspective of exam/quiz/homework, is Approach 2 considered optimal/better? Or both are considered same as overall time complexity remains O(n^2)? Approach 1 : Time to fill table is O(n^2). Time to extract result is O(n). Approach 2 : Time to fill table is O(n^2). Time to extract result is O(1). Assuming space is not a limiting factor in either. Also, assuming that filling the table can't improve beyond O(n^2). Comment by User 135758 on 2026-05-30 02:47 (Votes: 2) Both of these approaches would be eligible for full credit assuming the corresponding output procedures are matching. Comment by User 495006 on 2026-06-02 13:08 (Votes: 0) Would it be possible for the staff to release an example solution of how you would like the chain matrix multiple to be written in a way that gets full credit on an exam. Asking because it has all of the cases and conditions that would be hit in a dynamic programming question. For example, I'm assuming both of these two lines permissible: C(i,j) = min i≤k<j {C(i,k) + C(k +1,j) +mi−1 ·mk ·mj} C(i,j) = min{C(i,k) +C(k +1,j) +mi−1 ·mk ·mj : i ≤ k < j} but how do you represent an intermediate variable in the solution such as j =i+s Comment by User 135758 on 2026-06-02 13:37 (Votes: 0) The intermediate term s in the pseudocode is useful for controlling the iteration but isn't actually needed. Specifically, we control the iteration of i in reverse. Here's CMM pseudocode without s : for i = 1 to n: C[i, i] = 0 for j = 2 to n: for i = j - 1 to 1: C[i, j] = ∞ for k = i to j - 1: cur = C[i, k] + C[k+1, j] + m[i-1] * m[k] * m[j] if cost < C[i, j]: C[i, j] = cur return C[1, n] See the video walkthrough for DPV 6.7 for how this type of substring iteration manifests in the recurrence relation. Comment by User 649238 on 2026-06-04 07:48 (Votes: 0) Hello, I can't seem to find the guideline for this. For the extraction, if the problem asks to find the sequence, is pseudocode allowed here? I know we can write sentences as shown in the official solution. Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-04 09:25 (Votes: 1) https://edstem.org/us/courses/98593/discussion/8077940?comment=18704036 And https://edstem.org/us/courses/98593/discussion/8079608?comment=18709407 Comment by User 649238 on 2026-06-04 10:03 (Votes: 0) Thanks. i had full pseudocode for extraction and the grader commented that I should avoid pseudo code Your comment recommends little pseudo code is okay. So I guess sentences are safe. Comment by User 1664716 on 2026-06-09 01:58 (Votes: 0) Is it ok to prefill state tables with values like -Infinity , +Infinity ? Doing so made the recurrence easier to write in some cases, especially with min() , max() operations. Is defining a base like T[i]=0, -Infinity<i<=0 acceptable? This too made the recurrence succinct in some cases. Comment by User 135758 on 2026-06-09 21:01 (Votes: 1) ”pre-filling” sounds like a proposal which would later overwrite table values. This is not mathematically viable. Base-cases with infinite bounds would require infinite time to complete. This also does not sound viable for an optimal solution.

title: Graph Theory Guidance
text: Graph Theory Guidance Category : Staff Use Only > Supplemental Material Date : 2026-06-15 17:47 Link : https://edstem.org/us/courses/98593/discussion/8129087 Pinned : True | Votes : 3 | Views : 1437 Post Below you will find information on how you should approach solving Graph Theory problems in this class. Feel free to ask questions about writing a Graph Theory solution in this thread. Context A graph theory problem is a form of reduction . You are given some problem to solve, and the challenge is to solve that problem by using one of the graph algorithms we study this semester. In other words, you reduce your problem to a graph problem such that a known algorithm can solve it for you. The known algorithms (#192) are treated as a black-box - you are not allowed to change / modify them in any way. You can (and often will) modify the original problem input in some way or create a graph which represents the input - this becomes the input to the black-box. You then use the outputs from the black-box (possibly with modification) to output a solution to the original problem. Rules NO PSEUDOCODE - YOU WILL LOSE A LOT OF POINTS You may only use known black box algorithms (#192). You must use one or more black box algorithms (#192) to solve problems. You must not modify any black box algorithms (#192). Re-creating a black box with modifications is the same thing. All graphs are in adjacency list format (see below) You can assume you always have n and m for purposes of runtime analysis, where n represents the number of vertices |V| and m represents the number of edges |E|. #192 isn't exactly relevant here, but it's worth another link. See #8 for common course runtimes, including operations performed to graphs. Required Parts of a Graph Theory Solution (a) Algorithm Describe "how" to solve the problem in words (narrative/paragraph form) Bulleted steps are fine, but pseudocode/code is not allowed "Pseudocode" includes line-by-line restatement of code as words. If you find yourself using a lot of nested bullets, you might be erring on the side of line-by-line conversion of code into words, which is not a narrative. Describe what modifications are performed to the input , if any Detail the black box algorithm(s) being used What is passed in as input What is being used from its output Describe what modifications are performed to the output , if any Repeat as needed for any other black boxes Detail the final return for the problem's solution (b) Justification of Correctness Describe "why" your algorithm solves the problem, in words (narrative). This is not a formal inductive proof; informal justification is ok. Explain how your problem is solved by the black boxes used Explain how changing the inputs and/or outputs gets what you want (c) Runtime Analysis Analyze all steps of the algorithm in Big-O notation . Always, always in this course - worst case Big-O. Can explain/analyze in words and assert known black-box runtimes without further justification. Must include run time analysis for any pre/post processing See #8 for common runtimes when dealing with graphs. Provide an overall final runtime in (you guessed it) Big-O notation, fully simplified. If the problem specifies a target runtime, you must meet that for full credit. If we do not specify a runtime, faster (and correct) in Big O notation are worth more credit. While we work with worse-case runtimes, we also work with tightest-bound runtimes. That is, even though the worst case for an O(n+m) operation occurs when m= n^2, it is incorrect to state O(n^2) for such an operation unless we know something about the graph (e.g., it is a clique). O(n+m) is the tightest worse-case bound on such an operation Similarly, if we know the graph is a tree, then m = n-1 and O(n+m) operations collapse to O(n). When conveying the well-known runtimes of usable black boxes, you are not required to simplify it, even if the graph's constraints would allow for it. Graph Representation Graphs in this class, unless stated otherwise : Are simple graphs (no multi-edges or self-loops) Are always given in adjacency list format (see DPV 3.1.1) An array of vertices that are pointers to linked lists of adjacent vertices, such that each element in the list represents an edge to another vertex. Vertices are assumed to be labeled in such a way where they can be found by indexing into the array. Can be connected or disconnected, undirected or directed, sparse or dense If unstated by the problem, you should assume any of these could be true Are connected and undirected when working with MSTs Are connected and directed when working with flow networks When working with graphs, there are a number of common actions that can be presented without needing to go into details. Some examples as follows: Reversing a graph: "Reverse the edges in the graph". Copying a graph: "Create a copy of G and call it GCopy". Creating subgraphs: "Create a copy of G called GEven that only keeps edges with even numbered weights". "Create a copy of G called GK that only keeps vertices with a degree > k". "Create a residual graph of G called Grs that uses the flows from our run of EK". Unless the task can't directly be completed in this runtime, each of these are assumed to be O(n + m) operations. Please ask questions regarding the expectations for Graph Theory problems in this thread. Responses (7) Comment by User 821283 on 2026-06-18 14:29 (Votes: 2) Is that ok if my algorithm include 1 (or more) black box algorithm, but has also other non-trivial steps that traverse the graph? As an example, the 2nd part of the algorithm below is not a black box, but the 1st part is. Is that acceptable? Examples for 3.16 (minimum number of semesters necessary to complete the curriculum) Run topological sort on the graph. Under topological order, find the first vertex with incoming edges, remove all vertices before that from the graph, and add one semester. Repeat this step until graph is empty. Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-18 23:49 (Votes: 2) Yes, it's common that, as part of your solutions, there may be pre-processing or post-processing work that takes place around the black box usage. This could be creating subgraphs, modifying graphs, performing graph traversal, doing calculations, etc. Comment by User 813950 on 2026-06-19 08:41 (Votes: 0) I see that it says its graded; only this homework is graded? Comment by User 135758 on 2026-06-19 09:01 (Votes: 0) Is this for Homework 5? "Graded" generally means "marked for feedback". The weighting of those markings is unchanged from the syllabus. Comment by User 813950 on 2026-06-19 09:38 (Votes: 0) yes; sorry I got confused when i saw highlighted word graded. Thanks Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-19 09:43 (Votes: 0) Yes. If you make a submission, the graders grade and so it goes. Comment by User 585876 on 2026-06-19 23:11 (Votes: 0) Just to clarify wording: Similarly, if we know the graph is a tree, then m = n-1 and O(n+m) operations collapse to O(n). Is this saying that because we know that the graph is a tree, the tightest bound is O(n) or that even though we know it's a tree, the tightest bound should be reported as O(n+m) because that's what the operation runtime is Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-20 01:31 (Votes: 2) When it is a tree, we know that we have n vertices and exactly n-1 edges. If the input you are given is a tree, then O(n) and O(n + m) are the same, given that m has an exact definition, which enables simplification to O(n) . If the input you are given is not specified to be a tree (but we know it's connected), and you produce a tree (say with Kruskal's), then we have that m >= n-1 and O(n) becomes a tighter bound when performing work on the produced tree. Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-06-20 15:02 (Votes: 0) So just to clarify: Operate on the connected graph to produce your tree: O(m) but NOT O(n) (since graph is connected, m >= n-1) Operate on the produced tree: O(n) or O(m) (equivalent, because m = n - 1 for tree) Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-20 23:50 (Votes: 0) Operate on the produced tree: O(n) or O(m) (equivalent, because m = n - 1 for tree) For a produced tree - that is one like my example above, which could have come from a complete graph where m ~ n^2 - we have no assurance that m and n are equivalent. But we do know properties of a tree allow us to provide a tighter bound, if we go on to work on that tree. For a given tree - that is, the input to the problem is told to be a tree - then we do know they're equivalent, again based on a property of trees. Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-06-21 02:07 (Votes: 0) I think I was a bit loose on my definitions here, so let me clarify once more: Operate on a tree (m = n - 1 for tree): O(n+m) = O(n) = O(m). Operate on a generic connected graph (n-1 <= m <= n(n-1) for directed graph). So m = O(n^2) and n = O(m). Hence: O(n+m) = O(O(m) + m) = O(m). And also, O(n+m) = O(n + O(n^2)) = O(n^2). Comment by User 802900 on 2026-06-20 15:06 (Votes: 0) Why is the size of the adjacency list O(|E|) if each edge is represented twice? I would assume O(2|E|). Is this like runtime where we remove constant factors? Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-06-20 16:55 (Votes: 1) That's right, constant factors are ignored in Big-O notation. Just like how O(2n) == O(n). Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-06-20 16:56 (Votes: 0) I was looking at this example, and I was wondering if the task "find the vertex with largest degree" would have runtime: O(n) - if the metadata "number of edges" is stored on each vertex OR O(n+m) - if you need to count the number of edges manually But I'm not sure what is stored as metadata on each vertex? Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-20 23:55 (Votes: 1) The adjacency list, like our normal lists, do not store any metadata. So, no shortcuts on length finding. You'll see through the way the book and lectures talk, and when we get to the programming homework, that "metadata" such as lengths, weights, colors are actually separate structures entirely. The graph theory black boxes post in #192 also treats them this way. Given that, if you need to find the vertex with the largest degree, you'll need to count the number of neighbors for every vertex in the adjacency list, and you'd end up at O(n + m) overall. Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-06-21 01:42 (Votes: 0) Thank you Comment by User 1135584 on 2026-06-20 21:29 (Votes: 1) The lectures spend a lot of time on the proofs of correctness for these black box algorithms. The ed posts and homeworks make it seem like it will be important for us to know the inputs and outputs and generally what these blackboxes are doing so we can use them to solve graph problems. How important is it to study/memorize the proofs from the lectures? Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-21 00:00 (Votes: 0) How important is it to study/memorize the proofs from the lectures? The information Dr. Vigoda covers in the lectures for the proofs of correctness will prove quite insightful for student justification of correctness, just at "the next level". While you do not need to rederive the correctness of the black box, your solution will depend on some or all of its behavior, which you will have exploited in some way to solve the problem. That would be a great thing to include for why your algorithm works. And then of course, there's the entire portion of the course that isn't free response questions... Comment by User 1307404 on 2026-06-21 09:29 (Votes: 0) Can we modify an input graph G directly during the pre-processing stage or would we have to create a new graph G' before running our implementation? For example: we can remove an edge from G in O(1) time but creating a copy without the same edge could cost us O(n+m). Comment by User 135758 on 2026-06-21 10:18 (Votes: 2) Either could work, depending on whether or not G is needed again later in the algorithm.

title: Usable Black Boxes for Graphs
text: Usable Black Boxes for Graphs Category : Staff Use Only > Supplemental Material Date : 2026-06-15 17:48 Link : https://edstem.org/us/courses/98593/discussion/8129088 Pinned : True | Votes : 5 | Views : 1850 Post For the graphs section, you must use the algorithms presented in the course materials to help you solve presented problems. That is, solutions in this section must use one (or a combo) of the black boxes to solve the presented problem. Providing full implementation details of one of these black boxes, and adding in a twist or in-line tracking will be treated as a modification.Many graphs algorithms exist beyond what is covered in this course; however, only those explicitly mentioned here may be used. The use of extra-curricular algorithms will result in penalties, including for variations of these algorithms outside of the lectures, book, and this post.Wikipedia entries are provided for supplemental reading, such as history and discovery of these algorithms. Where differences exist, this post represents the version used in this course.All runtimes below are presented assuming n = |vertices| and m = |edges| .All outputs below are produced as n-sized lists, containing an entry for each vertex in the graph, and are able to be indexed by vertex in O(1) time to read its contents, unless otherwise noted.The following black boxes are available for use during the remainder of the course: Depth-First Search (DFS) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth-first_search ]- Input: A simple graph in adjacency list format A starting vertex This is optional. If not provided, DFS will start from an arbitrary location. This is accomplished through adjacency list ordering, which we assume takes place when you provide a starting vertex. Internal (not accessible after run) : visited[] - A list containing whether the indexed vertex was touched by DFS. All entries of this list will always be set to true when DFS completes. This is populated by Explore, an internal subroutine of DFS. Output: ccnum[] - A list containing the connected component number of the indexed vertex. Vertices reachable from the starting vertex will have a connected component number of 1 . prev[] - A list containing the parent vertex of the indexed vertex, which can be used to create a path from the starting vertex to any reachable vertex. Unreachable vertices and the starting vertex have a parent of nil . pre[] - A list containing the pre-visit number for the indexed vertex. post[] - A list containing the post-visit number for the indexed vertex. Runtime: O(n + m) Implementation details: DPV pp. 83-91 GR1.3, GR1.6 Common uses: Finding connected components on a graph Finding a cycle in a graph Producing a path from starting vertex to a reachable vertex Topological Sort (see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_sorting )- Input: A simple, directed, acyclic graph in adjacency list format Output: order[] - A list of vertices, sorted in topological ordering from source to sink. Note: This output is indexed numerically rather than by vertex. All outputs from the run of Depth-First Search (DFS) are also available to you. Runtime: O(n + m) Implementation details: DPV pp. 89-91 GR1.10 Common uses: Finding the topological sorting in a DAG Strongly Connected Components (SCC) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strongly_connected_component ]- Input: A simple, directed graph in adjacency list format Output: G_SCC = (V_SCC, E_SCC) - The strongly connected components metagraph, provided in adjacency list format. By construction, the metagraph is a DAG with vertices sorted from sink to source This ordering is known as reverse topological ordering. All outputs from the final run of Depth-First Search (DFS) are also available to you. This data is used to connect entities in the metagraph to the original input graph. For example, the first vertex in V_SCC represents all vertices with ccnum[v] = 1 from the DFS outputs from the original input graph. Runtime: O(n + m) Implementation details: DPV pp. 91-95 GR1.21 Common uses: Finding strongly connected components on a graph Particularly useful for finding source and sink SCCs Breadth-First Search (BFS) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadth-first_search ]- Input: A simple graph in adjacency list format A starting vertex Output: dist[] - A list containing the unweighted distance from the starting vertex to the indexed vertex for all vertices in the graph. Unreachable vertices have a distance of inf . prev[] - A list containing the parent vertex of the indexed vertex, which can be used to create a path from the starting vertex to any reachable vertex. Unreachable vertices and the starting vertex have a parent of nil . Runtime: O(n + m) Implementation details: DPV pp. 105-106 GR1.24 Common uses: Reachability analysis Unweighted shortest path determination Producing a path from starting vertex to a reachable vertex Dijkstra's (see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijkstra%27s_algorithm )- Input: A simple graph in adjacency list format A starting vertex A list of non-negative edge weights Output: dist[] - A list containing the weighted distance from the starting vertex to the indexed vertex for all vertices in the graph. Unreachable vertices have a distance of inf . prev[] - A list containing the parent vertex of the indexed vertex, which can be used to create a path from the starting vertex to any reachable vertex. Unreachable vertices and the starting vertex have a parent of nil . Runtime: O((n + m) log n) Implementation details: DPV pp. 109-115 GR1.24 Common uses: Reachability analysis Weighted shortest path determination Producing a path from starting vertex to a reachable vertex Bellman-Ford (BF) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellman%E2%80%93Ford_algorithm ]- Input: A simple graph in adjacency list format A starting vertex A list of edge weights Output: dist[] - A list containing the weighted distance from the starting vertex to the indexed vertex for all vertices in the graph. Unreachable vertices have a distance of inf . Values are based on the n-1 th iteration. prev[] - A list containing the parent vertex of the indexed vertex, which can be used to create a path from the starting vertex to any reachable vertex. Unreachable vertices and the starting vertex have a parent of nil . iter[][] - A 2-dimensional list containing the first indexed iteration's shortest path from the starting vertex to the second indexed vertex. For example, iter[3][v] contains the distance from the starting vertex to v at the end of the 3rd iteration. This table contains iterations 0 through n . Runtime: O(nm) Implementation details: DPV pp. 115-119 DP3.6 Common uses: Reachability analysis Weighted shortest path determination Negative cycle detection Producing a path from starting vertex to a reachable vertex Floyd-Warshall (FW) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floyd%E2%80%93Warshall_algorithm ]- Input: A simple graph in adjacency list format A list of edge weights Output: dist[][] - A 2-dimensional list containing the weighted distance from the first indexed vertex to the second indexed vertex. For example, dist[u][v] would contain the shortest path from vertex u to vertex v . Unreachable vertex pairs have a distance of inf . Values are based on the nth iteration. iter[][][] - A 3-dimensional list containing the first indexed iteration's shortest path from the second indexed vertex to the third indexed vertex. For example, iter[3][u][v] contains the distance from u to v at the end of the 3rd iteration. This table contains iterations 0 through n . Runtime: O(n^3) Implementation details: DPV pp. 172-173 DP3.17 Common uses: Reachability analysis Weighted shortest path determination Negative cycle detection Kruskal's (see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kruskal%27s_algorithm )- Input: A simple, connected, undirected graph in adjacency list format A list of edge weights Output: edges[] - A list of n-1 edges that represent a minimum spanning tree for the input graph. Runtime: O(m log n) Implementation details: DPV pp. 128-137 GR3.6 Common uses: Producing a minimum spanning tree Prim's (see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prim%27s_algorithm )- Input: A simple, connected, undirected graph in adjacency list format A list of edge weights Output: prev[] - A list containing the parent vertex of the indexed vertex, which represent the connecting edges of a minimum spanning tree for the input graph. The starting vertex is chosen arbitrarily and has a parent of nil . Runtime: O(m log n) Implementation details: DPV pp. 137-139 GR3.15 Common uses: Producing a minimum spanning tree Ford-Fulkerson (FF) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford%E2%80%93Fulkerson_algorithm ]- Input: A simple, connected, directed graph in adjacency list format A list of positive, integer edge capacities A starting source vertex A terminating sink vertex Output: flow[] - A list of edges representing the amount capacity used per each indexed edge such that the flow is maximized from the starting vertex to the terminating vertex. C - The value of the maximum flow from the starting vertex to the terminating vertex. Runtime: O(mC) Implementation details: DPV pp. 198-204 MF1.14 Common uses: Finding max flows on a graph Edmonds-Karp (EK) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonds%E2%80%93Karp_algorithm ]- Input: A simple, connected, directed graph in adjacency list format A list of positive edge capacities A starting source vertex A terminating sink vertex Output: flow[] - A list of edges representing the amount capacity used per each indexed edge such that the flow is maximized from the starting vertex to the terminating vertex. C - The value of the maximum flow from the starting vertex to the terminating vertex. Runtime: O(nm^2) Implementation details: DPV pp. 198-204 MF4.3 Common uses: Finding max flows on a graph 2-SAT (see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2-satisfiability )- Input: A Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form such that each clause contains at most 2 literals. This formula is backed by a list of n variables, representing at most 2n literals and m clauses. Output: assignments[] - A list indexable by the variables that back the original input formula containing whether that variable is set to true or false . If the input is not satisfiable, this will instead return "NO" All outputs from the Strongly Connected Components (SCC) run are also available to you. Runtime: O(n + m) Implementation details: DPV p. 101 GR2 Common uses: Example of how graphs algorithms can be used to solve a problem that starts in a non-graphs domain Converting a graph representation into a Boolean formula to determine satisfiability of the task at hand Responses (9) Comment by User 821283 on 2026-06-16 11:40 (Votes: 1) Thanks for posting this! This will include the list of black boxes available for use. For max flow algorithms, output flow[] is indexed by edge. The entries in flow[] are accessible in O(1) , the same as the entries in weight[] in the MST algorithms or shortest path algorithms. title: Week 4 — DP Shortest Paths + Graph Intro (SCC, 2-SAT)
text: Week 4 — DP Shortest Paths + Graph Intro (SCC, 2-SAT) Modules DP3 (Shortest Paths), GR1 (SCC), GR2 (2-SAT) · Exam 1 Window (covers Weeks 1–3) ◀ W03 Median · All weeks · Index · W05 MST ▶ EXAM 1 Window Assessment Exam 1 (format and scheduling per course syllabus) Coverage Weeks 1–3 — DP1–DP2, DC1–DC3 Watch the lecture (DP & Graph Intro) ▶ Open video · Transcript Learning objectives Run DFS , compute pre/post numbers, classify the four edge types, detect cycles, topologically sort. Find SCCs with the two-pass algorithm and explain why graph reversal works. Build a 2-SAT implication graph and decide satisfiability via SCCs. Choose the right shortest-path DP (Bellman-Ford / Floyd-Warshall / DAG) for weights and structure. Core concepts DFS and pre/post numbers — the graph foundation Definition. DFS stamps each vertex with a pre number (when first visited) and a post number (when finished). These intervals nest like parentheses. Topological sort (DAGs only): order vertices by decreasing post number. Cycle ⟺ a back edge exists — an edge ( u , v ) to an ancestor, i.e. with post[u] < post[v] . Four edge types (directed DFS): tree , back (to ancestor → cycle), forward (to descendant), cross (between subtrees). Strongly Connected Components (GR1) Definition. u ∼ v iff u reaches v and v reaches u . SCCs partition V ; the metagraph (contract each SCC) is always a DAG . Intuition: SCCs are the "two-way reachable" blobs; between blobs reachability is one-way. Source lemma: the vertex with the highest post number (in DFS on G R ) lies in a sink SCC of G . Peeling sink SCCs in that order isolates one SCC per DFS tree. 2-SAT (GR2) Definition. Decide a 2-CNF formula (each clause has 2 literals). Build the implication graph on 2 n literal vertices: clause ( a ∨ b ) adds the two implications ¬ a ⇒ b and ¬ b ⇒ a . Satisfiability criterion: f satisfiable ⇔ ∀ i , x i and ¬ x i lie in different SCCs . Intuition: if x i and ¬ x i are mutually reachable, the clauses force x i ⇒ ¬ x i and back — a contradiction. Shortest paths as DP (DP3) Bellman-Ford — DP over number of edges . Let dist ( k ) ( v ) = shortest s → v path using ≤ k edges: dist ( k ) ( v ) = min (dist ( k − 1) ( v ), min ( u , v ) ∈ E dist ( k − 1) ( u ) + w ( u , v )). Run k = 1… n − 1 . A further decrease at k = n means a negative cycle . Runtime O ( n m ) . Algorithms SCC decomposition (two-pass) — O ( n + m ) Run DFS on the reverse graph G R ; record post numbers. Process vertices of G in decreasing G R post order; each new DFS tree in G is one SCC. 2-SAT solver — O ( n + m ) Build the implication graph (2 implications per clause). Compute SCCs. If any x i , ¬ x i share an SCC → UNSAT . Else assign each variable by reverse topological SCC order (later SCC = true). Shortest-path chooser Algorithm Graph Negative weights Runtime BFS unweighted — O ( n + m ) Dijkstra non-negative weights no O (( n + m )log n ) Bellman-Ford (DP) general, detects neg cycles yes O ( n m ) Floyd-Warshall (DP) all-pairs yes (no neg cycle) O ( n 3 ) DAG shortest path DAG yes O ( n + m ) (topo order) Key theorems & results Cycle ⟺ back edge. DFS on G has a back edge iff G has a directed cycle. Metagraph is a DAG. Contracting SCCs never creates a cycle (else the blobs would merge). 2-SAT lemma. f is satisfiable iff no variable shares an SCC with its negation; assignment by reverse-topo SCC order is consistent. Worked example — SCC ordering Graph A → B → C → A (one SCC { A , B , C } ) plus C → D , D a sink. G R : A → C → B → A , D → C . DFS on G R gives highest post in { A , B , C } (a source SCC of G R = sink-side of G ). Processing G by decreasing G R post peels { A , B , C } first as one tree, then { D } . Metagraph: { A , B , C } → { D } — a DAG. Common pitfalls / exam traps Sorting by increasing post for topo order (it is decreasing ). Reducing graph problems by rewriting a black box's internals — instead transform input/output. Using Dijkstra with negative weights (invalid) — switch to Bellman-Ford. In 2-SAT, forgetting both implications per clause, or mis-assigning truth (later SCC in topo order = true). How to answer (HW / exam) Graph problems = transform input/output around a black box (DFS, SCC, BFS, Dijkstra). Don't rewrite the black box. See graph guidance · usable black boxes . Go deeper — readings · guidance · deep notes DPV §3.1–3.4 (graphs) · §4.x (paths) · §6.x (DP shortest path) Graph guidance · Black boxes · DP guidance Deep notes: GR0 fundamentals · GR1 SCC · GR2 2-SAT · cheat sheet lectures/ · transcripts/ · readings/ · guidance/ · notes/ Comprehensive Notes Full lecture notes for this week's modules (DP3 shortest paths, GR0 graph foundations, GR1 SCCs, GR2 2-SAT), with figures and diagrams inline. GR0 — Graph Fundamentals Graph. G = ( V , E ) : vertices V and edges E connecting pairs. Undirected edges are unordered { u , v } ; directed edges are ordered ( u , v ) (so A → B does not imply B → A ). We assume simple graphs (no self-loops, no parallel edges). Term Definition Degree deg ( v ) number of incident edges; in-/out-degree for directed Path / Cycle sequence of edges; cycle returns to start Connected (undirected) a path between every pair Strongly connected (directed) for every u , v : paths u → v and v → u DAG directed acyclic graph Source / Sink in-degree 0 / out-degree 0 Representations. Adjacency matrix : O ( n 2 ) space, O (1) edge lookup, O ( n ) to list neighbors. Adjacency list : O ( n + m ) space, O (deg ) lookup/iterate. This course uses adjacency lists (most graphs are sparse). BFS explores level by level and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, O ( n + m ) : BFS(G, s): for all v: dist[v] = ∞; prev[v] = null dist[s] = 0; Q = queue containing s while Q not empty: v = dequeue(Q) for all (v,w) ∈ E: if dist[w] = ∞: dist[w] = dist[v] + 1; prev[w] = v; enqueue(Q, w) Dijkstra = BFS for positive -weighted graphs, O ((| V |+| E |)log | V |) with a min-heap; it fails on negative weights (use Bellman-Ford). Key facts: any subpath of a shortest path is shortest; triangle inequality dist ( u , v ) ≤ dist ( u , x ) + dist ( x , v ) . DFS explores as deep as possible, backtracking — the foundation for SCCs, topological sort, and cycle detection. For directed graphs add a clock recording pre (discovery) and post (completion): Explore(z): pre[z] = clock++; visited[z] = true for all (z,w) ∈ E: if not visited[w]: Explore(w) post[z] = clock++ Pre/post intervals nest: if [pre( u ), post( u )] contains [pre( v ), post( v )] then u is an ancestor of v ; disjoint intervals mean neither is an ancestor. Edge types (directed DFS): tree, back (descendant→ancestor, the only type with post( z ) < post( w ) ), forward, cross. Theorem (cycle). G has a cycle ⇔ its DFS tree has a back edge . ( → ) the edge into the first-visited cycle vertex is a back edge; ( ← ) a back edge v → w plus the tree path w ⇝ v forms a cycle. Topological sort (DAGs only): run DFS, output vertices by decreasing post number , O ( n + m ) . Works because a DAG has no back edges, so every edge u → v has post( u ) > post( v ) . GR1 — Strongly Connected Components SCC. A maximal set of mutually strongly connected vertices ( v ⇝ w and w ⇝ v for all pairs). graph LR subgraph SCC1["SCC: A,B,E"] A --> B B --> E E --> A end subgraph SCC2["SCC: C,D"] C --> D D --> C end subgraph SCC3["SCC: F"] F end B --> C D --> F E --> F Metagraph. Collapse each SCC to a meta-vertex: the result is always a DAG (a cycle between two SCCs would merge them). Goal: find all SCCs in O ( n + m ) . Key insight. Running Explore(v) from a vertex in a sink SCC visits exactly that SCC — there are no outgoing metagraph edges to escape through. So: find a sink-SCC vertex, Explore it, remove it, repeat. Finding a sink SCC. We can't directly find a sink, but the vertex with the highest post number after DFS lies in a source SCC. Trick: run DFS on the reverse graph G R ( E R = {( w , v ) : ( v , w ) ∈ E } ) — SCCs are unchanged but sources and sinks swap, so the highest-post vertex in G R is in a source SCC of G R = sink SCC of G . SCC algorithm ( O ( n + m ) ): SCC(G): 1. Construct G^R (reverse all edges) 2. Run DFS(G^R) — compute post numbers 3. Order vertices by decreasing post number 4. Run DFS(G) in that order — each outer Explore call labels a new SCC Worked example. G : A → B , B → A , B → C , C → D , D → C , D → E (SCCs { A , B }, { C , D }, { E } , with { A , B } → { C , D } → { E } ). DFS on G R gives posts E (8), C (6), D (5), A (3), B (2) . Processing G in decreasing-post order E , C , D , A , B : Explore(E) → { E } (sink SCC), Explore(C) → C , D → { C , D } , Explore(A) → A , B → { A , B } . SCCs emerge sink-first (reverse topological order). Why it works (lemma). In DFS on G R , the highest-post vertex lies in a source SCC of G R (= sink SCC of G ). For SCCs S , S ′ with S ′ → S in G R 's metagraph: whichever is entered first by DFS, all of S finishes with a higher max-post than S ′ . So the globally-highest-post SCC is a source of G R . GR2 — 2-Satisfiability SAT / CNF. Boolean variables x 1 , …, x n ; literals x i and x̄ i . A CNF formula is an AND of OR-clauses; a satisfying assignment makes ≥ 1 literal true in every clause. k-SAT caps clause size at k : k = 2 is polynomial ( O ( n + m ) via SCCs); k ≥ 3 is NP-complete — one of the most important complexity boundaries. Implication graph. Each clause ( α ∨ β ) becomes two implications: if α is false then β must be true ( ᾱ → β ), and β̄ → α . Build 2 n literal vertices and 2 m edges: Clause Edges ( α ∨ β ) ᾱ → β , β̄ → α graph LR nx1["not-x1"] --> x2["x2"] nx2["not-x2"] --> x1["x1"] x1 --> x3["x3"] nx3["not-x3"] --> nx1 x2 --> nx3 x3 --> nx2 nx1 --> x3 nx3 --> x1 Key lemma (2-SAT). f is satisfiable ⇔ for every i , x i and x̄ i lie in different SCCs of the implication graph. (Same SCC means paths x i ⇝ x̄ i and x̄ i ⇝ x i — a contradiction either way.) Algorithm ( O ( n + m ) ): 2SAT(f): 1. Build implication graph (2n vertices, 2m edges) 2. Run SCC (sink-first order) 3. If any x_i, ¬x_i share an SCC → "unsatisfiable" 4. In reverse topological order, set each unassigned sink SCC's literals TRUE and their complements FALSE 5. Return assignment Correctness. Helper fact: a path α ⇝ β implies a path β̄ ⇝ ᾱ (each clause's two edges are complementary). Hence if S is a sink SCC, S̄ is a source SCC. Setting a sink SCC TRUE creates no outgoing-implication violations; its complement source set FALSE can imply anything vacuously. Worked example: f = ( x 1 ∨ x 2 ) ∧ ( x̄ 1 ∨ x 3 ) ∧ ( x̄ 2 ∨ x̄ 3 ) ∧ ( x 1 ∨ x 3 ) gives SCCs { x 1 , x 3 , x̄ 2 } and { x̄ 1 , x 2 , x̄ 3 } (complements), so it is satisfiable; assignment x 1 = T , x 2 = F , x 3 = T satisfies all clauses. DP3 — Shortest Paths (Dynamic Programming) Setting: a directed graph G⃗ = ( V , E ) with edge weights w ( e ) that may be negative , possibly with anti-parallel edges. For z ∈ V , dist ( z ) = length of the shortest path from s to z (an array of length n ). Dijkstra solves this in O (( n + m )log n ) but only for positive weights — it never revisits a vertex, so a later negative edge can't fix an already-finalized distance. Watch out — negative cycles. If a reachable cycle has negative total weight, repeatedly walking it lowers the path length without bound, so the shortest path is ill-defined. (A repeated-vertex route is a walk , not a path.) Generalized goal: find a negative-weight cycle reachable from s if one exists, else find dist ( z ) for all z (single-source shortest path). Bellman-Ford (single source) With no negative cycle, a shortest path visits each vertex at most once, so it has ≤ n − 1 edges. Condition on the number of edges : let D ( i , z ) = length of the shortest s → z path using ≤ i edges, 0 ≤ i ≤ n − 1 , z ∈ V . Base case: D (0, s ) = 0 and D (0, z ) = ∞ for z ≠ s . Recurrence (consider the last edge y → z , or use fewer edges): $$ D(i,z) = \min\Big\{\, D(i-1,z),\ \ \min_{y:\,\overrightarrow{yz}\in E}\big[D(i-1,y)+w(y,z)\big] \,\Big\}. $$ Bellman-Ford(G, s, w): for all z in V: D(0,z) = ∞ D(0,s) = 0 for i = 1 -> n-1: for all z in V: D(i,z) = D(i-1,z) for all edges (y,z) into z: if D(i,z) > D(i-1,y) + w(y,z): D(i,z) = D(i-1,y) + w(y,z) Return D(n-1, :) (Adjacency lists give edges out of a node; reverse once at O ( n + m ) to get edges into z .) Runtime: O ( n m ) — worse than Dijkstra but handles negative weights. Detecting a negative cycle. Run one extra round, to i = n . If D ( n , z ) < D ( n − 1, z ) for some z , a negative-weight cycle exists (backtrack to recover it); otherwise D ( n − 1, ⋅) is the answer. Floyd-Warshall (all pairs) Now find dist ( y , z ) for all pairs (no fixed source). Running Bellman-Ford from every vertex is O ( n 2 m ) = O ( n 4 ) worst case; Floyd-Warshall does it in O ( n 3 ) by conditioning on intermediate vertices . Let V = {1, …, n } and D ( i , s , t ) = length of the shortest s → t path using only {1, …, i } as intermediates. Base: D (0, s , t ) = w ( s , t ) if ( s , t ) ∈ E , else ∞ . D ( i , s , t ) = min { D ( i − 1, s , t ), D ( i − 1, s , i ) + D ( i − 1, i , t ) }. Floyd-Warshall(G, w): for s,t: D(0,s,t) = w(s,t) if (s,t)∈E else ∞ for i = 1 -> n: for s = 1 -> n: for t = 1 -> n: D(i,s,t) = min{ D(i-1,s,t), D(i-1,s,i) + D(i-1,i,t) } Return D(n, :, :) Runtime: O ( n 3 ) . Negative cycle ⇔ some diagonal entry D ( n , a , a ) < 0 (a negative path from a vertex to itself). Bellman-Ford vs Floyd-Warshall. Bellman-Ford from a fixed start d misses a negative cycle that d cannot reach; Floyd-Warshall examines all vertex pairs and always finds it. DPV chapter exercises DPV chapter exercises (exact, from the textbook) Exact end-of-chapter exercises, parsed from the DPV chapter PDFs. DPV Ch 3 — Decompositions Of Graphs — open exercises · chapter PDF DPV Ch 4 — Paths In Graphs — open exercises · chapter PDF DPV Ch 6 — Dynamic Programming — open exercises · chapter PDF Agent hint SCC/2-SAT/DFS question → DFS pre/post is the lever; topo = decreasing post; SCC = DFS on G R then G by decreasing post. For 2-SAT build the implication graph, run SCC, check x i vs ¬ x i . Deep walkthroughs in notes/ . Exam 1 (W1–3) opens this week.
