title: GR0: Graph Fundamentals
text:
GR0: Graph Fundamentals 📚 Reference: DPV Chapter 3 (Decompositions of Graphs) This is the foundation for everything. If you struggled with graphs before, this is where we fix that. 1. What Is a Graph? A graph G = (V, E) consists of: V — a set of vertices (aka nodes) E — a set of edges connecting pairs of vertices graph LR A --- B A --- C B --- C Two flavors: Undirected: edges are unordered pairs {u, v}. If A connects to B, then B connects to A. Directed: edges are ordered pairs (u, v). A → B does NOT mean B → A. graph LR A -->|directed| B A -->|directed| C B -->|directed| C We assume all graphs are simple — no self-loops (u, u) and no parallel edges. 2. Terminology Term Definition Adjacent Two vertices sharing an edge Neighborhood N(v) Set of vertices adjacent to v Degree deg(v) Number of edges incident to v; equals |N(v)| In-degree (directed) Number of edges coming into v Out-degree (directed) Number of edges going out of v Path Sequence of vertices connected by edges Cycle Path that starts and ends at the same vertex Connected (undirected) There's a path between every pair of vertices Strongly connected (directed) For every u, v: path from u→v AND v→u DAG Directed Acyclic Graph — directed graph with no cycles Source Vertex with in-degree 0 (nothing points to it) Sink Vertex with out-degree 0 (it points to nothing) ⚠️ Common Pitfall: In directed graphs, adjacency has direction. "A is adjacent to B" means there's an edge A → B. It does NOT mean B → A. 3. Graph Representations Adjacency Matrix An n × n matrix M where M[i][j] = 1 if edge (i, j) exists, 0 otherwise. Example (undirected): Example (directed): 1 2 3 1 2 3 1 [ 0 1 1 ] 1 [ 0 1 1 ] 2 [ 1 0 1 ] 2 [ 0 0 1 ] 3 [ 1 1 0 ] 3 [ 0 1 0 ] Space: O(n²) Check if edge exists: O(1) ✅ List all neighbors: O(n) ❌ Undirected → symmetric matrix Adjacency List Each vertex stores a list of its neighbors. Example (directed): 1 → [2, 3] 2 → [3] 3 → [2] Space: O(n + m) where m = |E| Check if edge exists: O(degree) ❌ List all neighbors: O(degree) ✅ 💡 Intuition: For sparse graphs (m ≪ n²), adjacency lists win. Most real-world graphs are sparse. This course uses adjacency lists unless stated otherwise. Adjacency Matrix Adjacency List Space O(n²) O(n + m) Edge lookup O(1) O(degree) Iterate neighbors O(n) O(degree) Best for Dense graphs Sparse graphs (most cases) 4. BFS: Breadth-First Search BFS explores the graph level by level, like ripples in a pond. It finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. BFS(G, s): Input: G = (V, E), source vertex s Output: dist[v] = min edges from s to v prev[v] = predecessor on shortest path for all v ∈ V: dist[v] = ∞ prev[v] = null dist[s] = 0 Q = queue containing s while Q is not empty: v = dequeue(Q) for all edges (v, w) ∈ E: if dist[w] = ∞: // not yet visited dist[w] = dist[v] + 1 prev[w] = v enqueue(Q, w) Runtime: O(n + m) — each vertex and edge visited once. BFS Example graph LR A((A
d=0)) --> B((B
d=1)) A --> C((C
d=1)) B --> D((D
d=2)) C --> D C --> E((E
d=2)) Starting from A: BFS visits {A} → {B, C} → {D, E} 🎯 Exam Tip: BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs only. For weighted graphs, you need Dijkstra's. 5. Dijkstra's Algorithm Dijkstra's is BFS for weighted graphs (with positive weights only). Dijkstra(G, s, w): Input: G = (V, E), source s, weights w(e) > 0 for all e Output: dist[v] = shortest weighted path from s to v prev[v] = predecessor on shortest path for all v ∈ V: dist[v] = ∞ prev[v] = null dist[s] = 0 H = min-heap with all vertices, keyed by dist while H is not empty: v = extractMin(H) for all edges (v, w) ∈ E: if dist[v] + w(v,w) < dist[w]: dist[w] = dist[v] + w(v,w) prev[w] = v decreaseKey(H, w) Runtime: O((|V| + |E|) log |V|) using a binary min-heap. Key lemmas: The subpath of any shortest path is itself a shortest path Triangle inequality: dist(u, v) ≤ dist(u, x) + dist(x, v) ⚠️ Common Pitfall: Dijkstra's does NOT work with negative edge weights. For negative weights, use Bellman-Ford (covered in DP3). 6. DFS: Depth-First Search (Undirected) DFS explores as deep as possible before backtracking. It's the foundation for SCCs, topological sort, and cycle detection. DFS for Finding Connected Components DFS(G): Input: G = (V, E) undirected, adjacency list Output: ccnum[v] = connected component number for each v cc = 0 for all v ∈ V: visited[v] = false for all v ∈ V: if not visited[v]: cc = cc + 1 Explore(v) Explore(z): visited[z] = true ccnum[z] = cc for all (z, w) ∈ E: if not visited[w]: Explore(w) Runtime: O(n + m) 💡 Intuition: Each call to Explore from the main DFS loop discovers a new connected component. Everything reachable from z gets the same cc number. graph TD subgraph "Component 1" A --- B B --- C end subgraph "Component 2" D --- E end subgraph "Component 3" F end 7. DFS for Directed Graphs — Pre/Post Numbering For directed graphs, we add a clock to track the order of discovery (pre) and completion (post) for each vertex. DFS(G): Input: G = (V, E) directed, adjacency list Output: pre[v], post[v] for each vertex clock = 1 for all v ∈ V: visited[v] = false for all v ∈ V: if not visited[v]: Explore(v) Explore(z): pre[z] = clock; clock++ visited[z] = true for all (z, w) ∈ E: if not visited[w]: Explore(w) post[z] = clock; clock++ Runtime: O(n + m) Worked Example graph LR A --> B A --> C B --> D B --> E D --> E E --> A Running DFS starting from A: Vertex pre post A 1 10 B 2 9 D 3 6 E 4 5 C 7 8 The pre/post intervals tell us about the tree structure: Containment: If [pre(u), post(u)] contains [pre(v), post(v)], then u is an ancestor of v Disjoint: If intervals don't overlap, neither is an ancestor of the other 8. Edge Types in DFS When we run DFS on a directed graph, every edge falls into exactly one of four categories: Edge Type Relationship Post Numbers Tree edge Parent → child in DFS tree post(z) > post(w) Back edge Descendant → ancestor post(z) < post(w) ⚠️ Forward edge Ancestor → non-child descendant post(z) > post(w) Cross edge Between unrelated vertices post(z) > post(w) graph TD A -->|tree| B A -->|tree| C B -->|tree| D D -->|back| A A -->|forward| D C -->|cross| D ⚠️ Common Pitfall: Back edges are the ONLY type where post(z) < post(w). For all other edges, post(z) > post(w). This is critical for understanding cycles and topological sort. The Cycle Theorem G has a cycle ⟺ its DFS tree has a back edge. Proof (→): Consider a cycle C. Let v_i be the first vertex of C visited by DFS. All other cycle vertices are reachable from v_i, so they become descendants. The edge v_{i-1} → v_i goes from descendant to ancestor = back edge. ✅ Proof (←): A back edge v → w means v is a descendant of w. So there's a path w ↝ v in the tree, plus the edge v → w. That's a cycle. ✅ 9. Topological Sorting A topological ordering of a DAG is a linear ordering of vertices such that for every edge u → v, u comes before v. 💡 Intuition: Think of it as a valid scheduling order. If task A must happen before task B, then A appears first. The Algorithm: Run DFS, then sort vertices by decreasing post number . TopologicalSort(G): Input: DAG G = (V, E) Output: vertices in topological order 1. Run DFS(G) to compute post numbers 2. Return vertices sorted by decreasing post[v] Why it works: In a DAG, there are no back edges. So for every edge u → v, post(u) > post(v). Sorting by decreasing post number gives a valid ordering. Runtime: O(n + m) for DFS + O(n) for sorting = O(n + m) Example graph LR X["X (post=10)"] --> Y["Y (post=8)"] X --> Z["Z (post=6)"] Y --> Z Z --> U["U (post=4)"] Z --> W["W (post=2)"] Topological order: X → Y → Z → U → W (sorted by decreasing post number) Alternative algorithm (useful conceptually): Find a sink vertex (no outgoing edges), output it Remove it from the graph Repeat until graph is empty Reverse the output list 🎯 Exam Tip: Topological sort only works on DAGs. If the graph has a cycle, topological ordering is impossible. (The existence of a back edge proves the cycle.) 10. Summary Table Algorithm Input Output Runtime Key Constraint BFS G, source s dist[], prev[] O(n + m) Unweighted edges Dijkstra's G, source s, weights dist[], prev[] O((V+E) log V) Positive weights only DFS (undirected) G ccnum[] O(n + m) — DFS (directed) G pre[], post[] O(n + m) — Topo Sort DAG G ordered vertices O(n + m) Must be a DAG Explore G, vertex v visited[] O(n + m) Finds all reachable from v 💡 The Big Picture: DFS is the Swiss Army knife of graph algorithms. Connected components, cycle detection, topological sorting, SCCs — they all build on DFS. Master DFS and the rest follows.

title: GR1: Strongly Connected Components
text: GR1: Strongly Connected Components 📚 Reference: DPV Chapter 3.4 SCCs are the directed-graph analog of connected components. The algorithm is elegant: just two passes of DFS. 1. Definition Strongly Connected: Vertices v and w are strongly connected if there's a path v ↝ w AND a path w ↝ v. Strongly Connected Component (SCC): A maximal set of mutually strongly connected vertices. "Maximal" means you can't add any more vertices and still have everyone strongly connected. graph LR subgraph SCC1["SCC: A,B,E"] A --> B B --> E E --> A end subgraph SCC2["SCC: C,D"] C --> D D --> C end subgraph SCC3["SCC: F"] F end B --> C D --> F E --> F This graph has 3 SCCs: {A, B, E}, {C, D}, and {F}. 2. The Metagraph — Every Directed Graph Is a DAG of Its SCCs If you collapse each SCC into a single "meta-vertex" and keep the edges between them, you get a DAG. graph LR S1["SCC: A,B,E"] --> S2["SCC: C,D"] S1 --> S3["SCC: F"] S2 --> S3 Key Property: The metagraph of SCCs is always a DAG. Why? If there were a cycle between two SCCs S and S', then every vertex in S could reach every vertex in S' and vice versa — meaning they should be merged into one bigger SCC. Contradiction. 3. The Goal We want to find all SCCs of a directed graph in O(n + m) time. Strategy: Think of the metagraph as a DAG. If we can identify the SCCs one at a time (say, starting from sinks), we can peel them off. Key insight: If we pick any vertex v in a sink SCC and run Explore(v), we visit exactly the vertices in that SCC (and nothing else — because a sink SCC has no outgoing edges in the metagraph). So the plan is: Find a vertex in a sink SCC Explore from it → discover the entire sink SCC Remove it Repeat 4. Finding a Sink SCC via the Reverse Graph Problem: How do we find a vertex guaranteed to be in a sink SCC? 💡 Intuition: We can't directly find a sink SCC, but we CAN find a source SCC — it's the one containing the vertex with the highest post number after DFS. And here's the trick: sources in G^R are sinks in G (and vice versa). G^R is the reverse graph — same vertices, all edges flipped: E^R = {(w, v) : (v, w) ∈ E} The SCCs are the same in G and G^R (reversing edges doesn't change strong connectivity). But sources and sinks swap! The Key Lemma Lemma: The vertex with the highest post number (from DFS on G^R) lies in a source SCC of G^R, which is a sink SCC of G . Proof sketch: For SCCs S and S' with an edge S → S' in the metagraph, the maximum post number in S is greater than the max post number in S'. The SCC with the globally highest post number must therefore be a source (nothing has a higher post number pointing into it). In G^R, this source corresponds to a sink in G. 5. The SCC Algorithm SCC(G): Input: Directed graph G = (V, E) Output: ccnum[v] = SCC number for each vertex 1. Construct G^R (reverse all edges) 2. Run DFS(G^R) — compute post numbers 3. Order vertices by decreasing post number 4. Run DFS(G) using this vertex ordering — each call to Explore from the main loop discovers a new SCC Runtime: O(n + m) Step 1: O(n + m) to construct reverse graph Step 2: O(n + m) for DFS Step 3: O(n) for ordering (or just process in decreasing order) Step 4: O(n + m) for DFS Why Step 4 Works In Step 4, we process vertices in decreasing post-number order from G^R. The first vertex we pick is in a sink SCC of G. Explore visits exactly that SCC (it can't escape — no outgoing metagraph edges). We mark it and continue. The next unvisited vertex with the highest remaining post number is in the next sink SCC (after removing the previous one). And so on. 6. Full Worked Example Consider this directed graph G: graph LR A --> B B --> C C --> A B --> D D --> E E --> D C --> E Step 1: Construct G^R (reverse all edges) graph LR B --> A C --> B A --> C D --> B E --> D D --> E E --> C Step 2: Run DFS on G^R (starting from, say, A) Vertex pre post A 1 10 C 2 9 B 3 8 D 4 7 E 5 6 Step 3: Order by decreasing post number A (10), C (9), B (8), D (7), E (6) Step 4: Run DFS on G (original) in this order Start with A → Explore finds: A → B → C → (A already visited) → D → E → (D already visited). Wait — this visits everything! Hmm, let me redo this more carefully. Let's use a different example where SCCs are clearer. Better Example graph LR A --> B B --> A B --> C C --> D D --> C D --> E SCCs: {A, B}, {C, D}, {E} Step 1: G^R: graph LR B --> A A --> B C --> B D --> C C --> D E --> D Step 2: DFS on G^R (start from A): Explore A → B → (A visited) → C → D → (C visited) → E → done backtracking. Vertex pre post A 1 10 B 2 9 C 3 8 D 4 7 E 5 6 Step 3: Order by decreasing post: A, B, C, D, E Step 4: DFS on G in this order: Explore(A): visits A → B → (A visited) → C → D → (C visited) → E Oops, this is because {A,B} can reach {C,D} can reach {E} OK — the trick is that the DFS in step 4 uses the undirected-style DFS (with component labeling). Each Explore call from the outer loop labels a new SCC. But within Explore, we only follow edges in G. Actually, let me reconsider. The key is that Step 4's DFS processes vertices in the order from Step 3. Since A has the highest post number in G^R, it's in a source SCC of G^R = sink SCC of G . But {A,B} is NOT a sink SCC here... Let me recheck. In G: {A,B} → {C,D} → {E}. So {E} is the sink SCC, {A,B} is the source. In G^R: edges are reversed, so {E} → {C,D} → {A,B}. So {A,B} is the sink SCC of G^R = source SCC of G^R... wait. The algorithm says: run DFS on G^R to find vertex ordering, then run DFS on G . The vertex with the highest post in G^R is in a source SCC of G^R = source SCC of G^R . But we want to find sink SCCs of G = source SCCs of G^R . ✅ So in G^R, vertex A has post=10 (highest). A is in a source SCC of G^R. Source of G^R = Sink of G... but {A,B} is NOT the sink of G! Let me reconsider: In G^R: {A,B} has an incoming edge from C (C→B in G^R). So {A,B} is NOT a source in G^R. {E} has an outgoing edge E→D in G^R, and incoming? Nothing points to E in G^R. So {E} is a source in G^R. But E has post=6, the LOWEST. I think the issue is my DFS traversal on G^R. Let me redo it starting from E: DFS on G^R starting from E: Explore(E): E → D → C → B → A → (B visited, back to A) → (back up) ... Starting vertex choice matters! DFS iterates over ALL vertices. Let's say the outer loop goes A, B, C, D, E: Explore(A): A → B (in G^R, edges from A are: A→C via C→A reversed? No: G has A→B, B→A, B→C, C→D, D→C, D→E. So G^R has: B→A, A→B, C→B, D→C, C→D, E→D. G^R adjacency list: A: [B] (from B→A in G^R; because A→B in G) B: [A] (from A→B in G^R; because B→A in G) C: [B, D] (from B→C reversed gives C→B; D→C reversed gives C→D) D: [C, E] (from C→D reversed gives D→C; but wait... C→D in G means D→C in G^R. And D→E in G means E→D in G^R) Let me redo: G edges: A→B, B→A, B→C, C→D, D→C, D→E G^R edges: B→A, A→B, C→B, D→C, C→D, E→D G^R adjacency list: A: [B] B: [A] C: [B, D] D: [C] E: [D] DFS on G^R, outer loop order A, B, C, D, E: Explore(A): visit A, go to B. Visit B, go to A (visited). Backtrack. post(B)=2, post(A)=3. B already visited. Skip. Explore(C): visit C, go to B (visited), go to D. Visit D, go to C (visited). Backtrack. post(D)=5, post(C)=6. D already visited. Skip. Explore(E): visit E, go to D (visited). Backtrack. post(E)=8. Vertex post A 3 B 2 C 6 D 5 E 8 Step 3: Order by decreasing post: E(8), C(6), D(5), A(3), B(2) Step 4: DFS on G (original), process in order E, C, D, A, B: G adjacency list: A: [B] B: [A, C] C: [D] D: [C, E] E: [] Explore(E): visit E. No outgoing edges. SCC 1 = {E} ✅ (sink SCC!) Explore(C): visit C → D → C (visited) → E (visited). Backtrack. SCC 2 = {C, D} ✅ D already visited. Skip. Explore(A): visit A → B → A (visited) → C (visited). Backtrack. SCC 3 = {A, B} ✅ B already visited. Skip. Result: SCCs are {E}, {C, D}, {A, B} — found in reverse topological order (sink first). ✅ 7. The Proof — Why This Works The Core Claim Claim: For SCCs S and S', if there's an edge from S to S' in the metagraph, then: max post-number in S > max post-number in S' (in the DFS on G^R) Wait — actually the claim is stated for G^R's DFS. Let me state it precisely. Lemma: In DFS on G^R, the vertex with the highest post number lies in a source SCC of G^R (= sink SCC of G). Proof: Consider two SCCs S and S' where S' → S is an edge in G^R's metagraph (meaning S → S' in G's metagraph). Let u be the first vertex visited (by DFS on G^R) among all vertices in S ∪ S'. Case 1: u ∈ S. Then from u, DFS can reach all of S (since S is an SCC). DFS will finish all of S before it can possibly finish exploring from u. But S has an edge to S' in G^R's metagraph, so DFS might also reach S'. Either way, post(u) ≥ max post in S', and u ∈ S, so max post in S > max post in S'. Case 2: u ∈ S'. Then DFS explores all of S' from u. But S' has no edge to S in G^R, so DFS won't reach S from within S'. All of S' finishes before any of S is visited. So max post in S > max post in S'. In both cases, max post in S > max post in S'. The SCC with the globally highest post number has no SCC with a higher max-post pointing to it → it's a source in G^R → sink in G. ✅ 8. DFS vs Explore — An Important Distinction DFS Explore Visits ALL vertices Only vertices reachable from v Uses source vertex? No (iterates over all) Yes (starts from v) Output pre/post for everyone visited[] for reachable vertices 🎯 Exam Tip: Explore(v) in a sink SCC visits exactly that SCC and nothing else. This is why the SCC algorithm works — we pick vertices in sink SCCs first, Explore them, mark them done, and move on. 9. Summary Property Value Algorithm 2 passes of DFS (one on G^R, one on G) Runtime O(n + m) Key idea Highest post in G^R → sink SCC of G Metagraph Always a DAG Output SCC labels + topological ordering of SCCs

title: GR2: 2-Satisfiability (2-SAT)
text: GR2: 2-Satisfiability (2-SAT) 📚 Reference: DPV Chapter 3.4 (Applications of SCC) This is a beautiful application of SCCs. We reduce a logic problem to a graph problem and solve it in linear time. 1. SAT and CNF — The Setup Boolean Formulas We work with boolean variables x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ, each either TRUE (1) or FALSE (0). For each variable xᵢ, we have two literals : xᵢ and x̄ᵢ (its negation/complement). Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF) A formula in CNF is an AND of OR-clauses: f = ( x 2 ) ∧ ( x̄ 3 ∨ x 4 ) ∧ ( x 3 ∨ x̄ 5 ∨ x̄ 1 ∨ x 2 ) Clause: An OR (∨) of literals, e.g., (x₃ ∨ x̄₅ ∨ x̄₁) Formula: An AND (∧) of clauses Satisfying assignment: Values for each variable that make the entire formula TRUE This means at least one literal in every clause must be TRUE The SAT Problem Input: A formula f in CNF with n variables and m clauses Output: A satisfying assignment, or "NO" if none exists 2. k-SAT k-SAT restricts every clause to have at most k literals . k Complexity 1 Trivial (each clause forces a variable) 2 Polynomial — O(n + m) via SCCs! 3+ NP-complete (no known polynomial algorithm) The jump from k=2 to k=3 is one of the most important complexity boundaries in CS. We're going to solve 2-SAT. 3. The Implication Graph Here's the key idea: every 2-SAT clause can be rewritten as two implications . For a clause (α ∨ β): If α is FALSE, then β MUST be TRUE → implication: ᾱ → β If β is FALSE, then α MUST be TRUE → implication: β̄ → α Construction Given a 2-SAT formula with n variables and m clauses: Vertices: 2n vertices — one for each literal xᵢ and x̄ᵢ Edges: 2m directed edges — two implications per clause Clause Edge 1 Edge 2 (α ∨ β) ᾱ → β β̄ → α Example f = ( x̄ 1 ∨ x̄ 2 ) ∧ ( x 2 ∨ x 3 ) ∧ ( x̄ 3 ∨ x̄ 1 ) Clause Implications Edges (x̄₁ ∨ x̄₂) x₁ → x̄₂, x₂ → x̄₁ x₁ → x̄₂, x₂ → x̄₁ (x₂ ∨ x₃) x̄₂ → x₃, x̄₃ → x₂ x̄₂ → x₃, x̄₃ → x₂ (x̄₃ ∨ x̄₁) x₃ → x̄₁, x₁ → x̄₃ x₃ → x̄₁, x₁ → x̄₃ graph LR x1["x1"] --> nx2["not-x2"] x2["x2"] --> nx1["not-x1"] nx2 --> x3["x3"] nx3["not-x3"] --> x2 x3 --> nx1 x1 --> nx3 💡 Intuition: Paths in this graph are chains of logical implications. If there's a path x₁ ↝ x̄₁, it means "if x₁ is TRUE, then x₁ must be FALSE" — a contradiction (unless x₁ is just FALSE). 4. The Key Lemma Lemma: A 2-SAT formula f is satisfiable if and only if for all i, xᵢ and x̄ᵢ are in different SCCs of the implication graph. Equivalently: f is unsatisfiable ⟺ there exists some i where xᵢ and x̄ᵢ are in the same SCC. Why "same SCC = unsatisfiable" If xᵢ and x̄ᵢ are in the same SCC, then: There's a path xᵢ ↝ x̄ᵢ (if xᵢ is TRUE, then x̄ᵢ must be TRUE → contradiction) There's a path x̄ᵢ ↝ xᵢ (if x̄ᵢ is TRUE, then xᵢ must be TRUE → same contradiction) Neither assignment works → unsatisfiable Why "different SCCs = satisfiable" This is the harder direction. We need to actually construct a satisfying assignment. That's where the algorithm comes in. 5. The 2-SAT Algorithm 2SAT(f): Input: Formula f in 2-CNF with n variables, m clauses Output: Satisfying assignment or "unsatisfiable" 1. Construct the implication graph G (2n vertices, 2m edges) 2. Run SCC algorithm on G → get SCCs in reverse topological order (sink first) 3. For each i: if xᵢ and x̄ᵢ are in the same SCC, return "unsatisfiable" 4. For each SCC S (in reverse topological order, sink → source): - If literals in S are unassigned: - Set all literals in S to TRUE - Set all complement literals (in S̄) to FALSE 5. Return assignment Runtime: O(n + m) — dominated by the SCC computation. 6. Why the Algorithm Is Correct The Assignment Strategy 💡 Intuition: Sink SCCs are "safe" to set TRUE because they have no outgoing implications to worry about. Their complements are source SCCs (safe to set FALSE because FALSE can imply anything). Claim: If S is a sink SCC, then S̄ is a source SCC Proof: First, we need a helper fact: Fact: If there's a path α ↝ β in the implication graph, then there's a path β̄ ↝ ᾱ. Why? Each edge ᾱ → β in the implication graph came from a clause (α ∨ β), which also produced the edge β̄ → ᾱ. Chaining these along a path gives us the complement path in reverse. Now, suppose S is a sink SCC. For any α ∈ S: There's no edge from α to any vertex outside S (sink property) By the helper fact, there's no edge from any vertex outside S̄ to ᾱ So S̄ has no incoming edges from outside → S̄ is a source SCC ✅ Why Setting Sink = TRUE Works When we set a sink SCC S to TRUE: S has no outgoing edges → no implications to propagate S̄ is set to FALSE. S̄ is a source → all edges from S̄ go outward. But FALSE can imply anything (FALSE → anything is vacuously TRUE), so no contradictions arise. After removing S and S̄, the remaining graph still has valid SCCs, and we repeat. 7. Worked Example f = ( x 1 ∨ x 2 ) ∧ ( x̄ 1 ∨ x 3 ) ∧ ( x̄ 2 ∨ x̄ 3 ) ∧ ( x 1 ∨ x 3 ) Step 1: Build implication graph Clause Edge 1 Edge 2 (x₁ ∨ x₂) x̄₁ → x₂ x̄₂ → x₁ (x̄₁ ∨ x₃) x₁ → x₃ x̄₃ → x̄₁ (x̄₂ ∨ x̄₃) x₂ → x̄₃ x₃ → x̄₂ (x₁ ∨ x₃) x̄₁ → x₃ x̄₃ → x₁ graph LR nx1["not-x1"] --> x2["x2"] nx2["not-x2"] --> x1["x1"] x1 --> x3["x3"] nx3["not-x3"] --> nx1 x2 --> nx3 x3 --> nx2 nx1 --> x3 nx3 --> x1 Step 2: Find SCCs Let's trace the paths: x̄₁ → x₂ → x̄₃ → x₁ → x₃ → x̄₂ → x₁ (cycle: x₁, x₃, x̄₂, x̄₃ form paths but let's check) x̄₃ → x̄₁ → x₃ (via x̄₁ → x₃) — and x₃ → x̄₂ → x₁ → x₃ (cycle!) SCC analysis: x₁ → x₃ → x̄₂ → x₁: SCC A = {x₁, x₃, x̄₂} x̄₁ → x₂ → x̄₃ → x̄₁: SCC B = {x̄₁, x₂, x̄₃} Note: SCC A and SCC B are complements of each other! ✅ Step 3: Check — no xᵢ and x̄ᵢ in the same SCC. ✅ Satisfiable! Step 4: Assign SCC A = {x₁, x₃, x̄₂} and SCC B = {x̄₁, x₂, x̄₃} Which is the sink? A has edges: x₁ → x₃ (internal), x₃ → x̄₂ (internal), x̄₂ → x₁ (internal). Any outgoing? Check all edges from members of A to non-members... If A is the sink: Set SCC A = TRUE: x₁ = T, x₃ = T, x̄₂ = T → x₂ = F Set SCC B = FALSE: x̄₁ = F, x₂ = F, x̄₃ = F → x₁ = T, x₃ = T ✅ (consistent!) Verify: x₁ = T, x₂ = F, x₃ = T (x₁ ∨ x₂) = (T ∨ F) = T ✅ (x̄₁ ∨ x₃) = (F ∨ T) = T ✅ (x̄₂ ∨ x̄₃) = (T ∨ F) = T ✅ (x₁ ∨ x₃) = (T ∨ T) = T ✅ 8. Unit Clause Simplification (Preprocessing) If a clause has only one literal (a unit clause), we can simplify: Find unit clause with literal α Set α = TRUE Remove all clauses containing α Remove ᾱ from all remaining clauses (may create new unit clauses or empty clauses) If any clause becomes empty → unsatisfiable Repeat This preprocessing reduces the problem before building the implication graph. After removing all unit clauses, every clause has exactly 2 literals. 9. Summary Problem Given 2-CNF formula, find satisfying assignment Key idea Build implication graph, run SCC Satisfiable iff No xᵢ and x̄ᵢ in same SCC Assignment Sink SCC → TRUE, its complement (source) → FALSE Runtime O(n + m) Contrast 3-SAT is NP-complete! 🎯 Exam Tip: The construction of the implication graph is the critical step. Remember: clause (α ∨ β) gives edges ᾱ → β and β̄ → α. Each clause contributes exactly 2 edges. ⚠️ Common Pitfall: Don't confuse the implication graph edges. For (α ∨ β), the implication is "if NOT α, then β" — so the edge goes from ᾱ to β, not from α.

title: GR3: Minimum Spanning Tree
text: GR3: Minimum Spanning Tree 📚 Reference: DPV Chapter 5.1 (Greedy Algorithms — MST) MST is our first greedy algorithm that provably works. The key is the Cut Property. 1. Problem Definition Given: An undirected, connected graph G = (V, E) with edge weights w(e) Find: A spanning tree T ⊆ E of minimum total weight: min Σ w(e) for e ∈ T A spanning tree of G is a subset of edges that: Connects all vertices (spans the graph) Has no cycles (it's a tree) Has exactly |V| - 1 edges 2. Tree Properties These three properties are equivalent for a subgraph with n vertices: Property Meaning Connected + n-1 edges → Must be a tree Connected + acyclic → Must have n-1 edges n-1 edges + acyclic → Must be connected Also important: A tree has exactly one path between any pair of vertices Removing any edge disconnects a tree Adding any edge to a tree creates exactly one cycle 💡 Intuition: A tree is the most economical way to keep a graph connected — it uses the minimum number of edges (n-1). An MST does this with minimum total weight. 3. Kruskal's Algorithm Repeatedly add the lightest edge that doesn't create a cycle. Kruskal(G, w): Input: Undirected graph G = (V, E) with weights w(e) Output: MST edge set X 1. Sort E by increasing weight 2. X = ∅ 3. For each edge e = (v, w) in sorted order: if adding e to X doesn't create a cycle: X = X ∪ {e} 4. Return X Cycle Detection with Union-Find How do we efficiently check "does adding (v, w) create a cycle"? Use a Union-Find (disjoint set) data structure: Find(v): Returns the component containing v Union(v, w): Merges the components of v and w Adding edge (v, w) creates a cycle ⟺ Find(v) = Find(w) (already in same component). Kruskal(G, w): // with Union-Find 1. Sort E by increasing weight 2. X = ∅ 3. Initialize Union-Find with each vertex in its own set 4. For each edge e = (v, w) in sorted order: if Find(v) ≠ Find(w): X = X ∪ {e} Union(v, w) 5. Return X Runtime: O(|E| log |V|) Sorting: O(|E| log |E|) = O(|E| log |V|) since |E| ≤ |V|² Union-Find operations: O(|E| · α(|V|)) ≈ O(|E|) (nearly constant per op) Dominated by sorting Worked Example graph LR A ---|1| B A ---|4| C B ---|2| C B ---|3| D C ---|5| D C ---|7| E D ---|6| E Sorted edges: (A,B,1), (B,C,2), (B,D,3), (A,C,4), (C,D,5), (D,E,6), (C,E,7) Step Edge Weight Add? Reason 1 (A,B) 1 ✅ Different components 2 (B,C) 2 ✅ Different components 3 (B,D) 3 ✅ Different components 4 (A,C) 4 ❌ Same component — would create cycle 5 (C,D) 5 ❌ Same component 6 (D,E) 6 ✅ Different components. Done! (4 edges = n-1) MST edges: {(A,B), (B,C), (B,D), (D,E)} with total weight = 1+2+3+6 = 12 graph LR A ---|1| B B ---|2| C B ---|3| D D ---|6| E style A fill:#90EE90 style B fill:#90EE90 style C fill:#90EE90 style D fill:#90EE90 style E fill:#90EE90 4. The Cut Property — Why Kruskal's Works What Is a Cut? Definition: For an undirected graph G = (V, E), a cut is a partition of V into two non-empty sets S and S̄ = V \ S. The cut edges are: cut(S, S̄) = {(v, w) ∈ E : v ∈ S, w ∈ S̄} graph LR subgraph S_set["S"] A B end subgraph Sbar["S-bar"] C D E end A ---|"cut edge"| C B ---|"cut edge"| D A --- B C --- D D --- E The Cut Property Lemma Lemma (Cut Property): Let X ⊆ E be a subset of some MST T. Let S ⊆ V be such that no edge of X crosses the cut (S, S̄). Let e* be a minimum weight edge crossing the cut. Then X ∪ {e*} ⊆ T' for some MST T'. In plain English: A minimum-weight edge across any cut is safe to add to the MST. 💡 Intuition: If I give you any tree T that doesn't include e*, I can swap e* in and some other cut edge out, and the weight won't increase (because e* is the lightest across the cut). So there's always an MST containing e*. Proof of the Cut Property Setup: Fix G, X, T (an MST containing X), and S. e* is a min-weight edge in cut(S, S̄) No edge of X crosses the cut Goal: Show X ∪ {e*} ⊆ T' for some MST T'. Case A: e* ∈ T. Then T' = T. Done. ✅ Case B: e* ∉ T. We construct T'. Add e* to T → creates a unique cycle C (since T is a tree) e* = (a, b) crosses the cut (a ∈ S, b ∈ S̄). The cycle C must cross the cut at least one more time (to get back from S̄ to S). Let e' be another edge of C that crosses the cut. Set T' = T ∪ {e*} \ {e'} Claim 1: T' is a tree. T' has n-1 edges (added one, removed one) T' is connected: any path in T that used e' can detour through the rest of cycle C (which includes e*) Connected + n-1 edges → tree ✅ Claim 2: T' is an MST. w(e*) ≤ w(e') because e* is minimum weight across the cut and e' also crosses the cut w(T') = w(T) + w(e*) - w(e') ≤ w(T) But T is already minimum weight, so w(T') = w(T) ✅ Claim 3: X ∪ {e } ⊆ T'. * X ⊆ T and X has no edges crossing the cut, so e' ∉ X, meaning X ⊆ T' = T \ {e'} ∪ {e*} e* ∈ T' by construction ✅ 🎯 Exam Tip: The proof of the Cut Property is one of the most likely proof questions on the exam. Know the two cases (e* in T or not) and the swap argument. 5. Why Kruskal's Is Correct (via Cut Property) At each step of Kruskal's, when we add edge e = (v, w): v and w are in different components (otherwise we'd skip) Let S = the component containing v, S̄ = everything else No edge of X (edges added so far) crosses this cut (by definition of components) e is the minimum weight edge crossing this cut (because we process edges in sorted order — all lighter edges either don't cross this cut or were already added) By the Cut Property, adding e is safe ✅ By induction, X is always a subset of some MST. When |X| = n-1, X IS that MST. 6. Prim's Algorithm Prim's grows a single tree from a starting vertex, always adding the lightest edge connecting the tree to a non-tree vertex. Prim(G, w): Input: Undirected graph G = (V, E) with weights w(e) Output: MST edge set X X = ∅ S = {any starting vertex} while |X| < |V| - 1: e* = minimum weight edge in cut(S, V\S) X = X ∪ {e*} S = S ∪ {endpoint of e* in V\S} Return X Implementation: Use a min-heap keyed by the lightest edge connecting each non-tree vertex to the tree. Runtime: O(|E| log |V|) with binary heap Correctness: Direct application of the Cut Property at each step (S = tree vertices so far, no edge of X leaves S since the tree is contained in S). Prim's Example Same graph as before, starting from A: graph LR A ---|1| B A ---|4| C B ---|2| C B ---|3| D C ---|5| D C ---|7| E D ---|6| E Step S (tree) Lightest cut edge Add 1 {A} (A,B) w=1 (A,B) 2 {A,B} (B,C) w=2 (B,C) 3 {A,B,C} (B,D) w=3 (B,D) 4 {A,B,C,D} (D,E) w=6 (D,E) Same MST: {(A,B), (B,C), (B,D), (D,E)}, weight = 12 ✅ 7. Kruskal's vs Prim's Kruskal's Prim's Strategy Global: lightest edge overall Local: lightest edge from current tree Grows Forest → single tree Single tree from start Data structure Union-Find Min-heap Runtime O(|E| log |V|) O(|E| log |V|) Better for Sparse graphs Dense graphs Correctness Cut Property (S = component) Cut Property (S = tree so far) Both are just special cases of the generic "greedy + Cut Property" approach. ⚠️ Common Pitfall: MST is for undirected graphs only. The directed analog (minimum spanning arborescence) is a completely different problem. ⚠️ Common Pitfall: If multiple edges have the same weight, the MST may not be unique — but the total weight is. Any tie-breaking in Kruskal's or Prim's yields a valid MST. 8. Summary Problem Find minimum-weight spanning tree Key Lemma Cut Property: min-weight edge across any cut is in some MST Kruskal's Sort edges, greedily add lightest non-cycle edge. O(|E| log |V|) Prim's Grow tree from root, add lightest cut edge. O(|E| log |V|) Proof technique Swap argument: add e*, remove another cut edge, weight doesn't increase Tree facts n-1 edges, connected, acyclic (any 2 of 3 imply the third)

title: GR4: Markov Chains & PageRank
text:
GR4: Markov Chains & PageRank This module connects graph theory, linear algebra, and probability. PageRank uses all three to define the "importance" of a webpage. The key insight: importance = stationary distribution of a random walk. 1. What Is a Markov Chain? A Markov chain is a random process that moves between states over discrete time steps, where the next state depends only on the current state (not the history). Formally: N states: {1, 2, ..., N} Transition matrix P (N × N): P(i, j) = Pr(go from state i to state j) Two key constraints on P: P(i, j) ∈ [0, 1] for all i, j (probabilities) Each row sums to 1: Σⱼ P(i, j) = 1 (from any state, you go somewhere ) A matrix with non-negative entries where every row sums to 1 is called a stochastic matrix . Example: The CS 6210 Student graph LR K["Kishore
(lecture)"] -->|0.5| K K -->|0.5| E["Check
Email"] E -->|0.2| K E -->|0.5| S["StarCraft"] E -->|0.3| Z["Sleep"] S -->|0.3| E S -->|0.7| S Z -->|0.7| K Z -->|0.3| Z Note: self-loops are allowed (and common) in Markov chains! Transition matrix: Kishore Email StarCraft Sleep Kishore [ 0.5 0.5 0 0 ] Email [ 0.2 0 0.5 0.3 ] StarCft [ 0 0.3 0.7 0 ] Sleep [ 0.7 0 0 0.3 ] Each row sums to 1. ✅ 2. k-Step Transitions: Powers of P One step: P(i, j) = probability of going from i to j in 1 step. Two steps: P²(i, j) = probability of going from i to j in exactly 2 steps . k steps: Pᵏ(i, j) = probability of going from i to j in exactly k steps. 💡 Intuition: Matrix multiplication naturally sums over all possible intermediate states — exactly what we need for multi-step probabilities. Example: P² for the 6210 chain P² = [ 0.35 0.25 0.25 0.15 ] [ 0.31 0.25 0.35 0.09 ] [ 0.06 0.21 0.64 0.09 ] [ 0.56 0.15 0 0.09 ] (approximate) Verification: P²(2, 1) = Pr(Email → Kishore in 2 steps) = (Email → Kishore → Kishore) + (Email → Sleep → Kishore) = (0.2)(0.5) + (0.3)(0.7) = 0.10 + 0.21 = 0.31 ✅ 3. What Happens for Large k? Something remarkable: as k → ∞, the rows of Pᵏ all converge to the same vector . For our example, P²⁰ ≈ [ 0.292 0.188 0.406 0.104 ] [ 0.292 0.188 0.406 0.104 ] [ 0.292 0.188 0.406 0.104 ] [ 0.292 0.188 0.406 0.104 ] Every row is approximately π = [0.292, 0.188, 0.406, 0.104] . What this means: No matter where you start, after enough time steps, the probability of being in each state converges to π. You'll spend ~29.2% of your time listening to Kishore, ~40.6% playing StarCraft, etc. — regardless of starting state . This π is the stationary distribution . 4. Stationary Distribution Definition: A stationary distribution π is a row vector such that πP = π . In other words: if you're in distribution π and take one step, you stay in π. It's a fixed point of the random walk. Linear Algebra Perspective πP = π means π is a left eigenvector of P with eigenvalue 1 . More generally, if μ₀ is your initial distribution (a row vector), then: After 1 step: μ₁ = μ₀ · P After 2 steps: μ₂ = μ₀ · P² After k steps: μₖ = μ₀ · Pᵏ As k → ∞, μₖ → π regardless of μ₀ (under the right conditions). Key Questions Does every Markov chain have a stationary distribution? Is it unique? Do we always converge to it? The answer to all three is yes — if the chain is ergodic . 5. Ergodic Markov Chains A Markov chain is ergodic if it's both: (a) Irreducible (= Strongly Connected) The underlying directed graph is one strongly connected component — you can get from any state to any other state. ⚠️ Pitfall: If there are multiple SCCs, the starting state determines which states you can reach. No unique stationary distribution. graph LR subgraph SCC1 A --> B --> A end subgraph SCC2 C --> D --> C end This is NOT irreducible — starting in SCC1, you never reach SCC2. Fix: Make the graph fully connected (positive probability between every pair). (b) Aperiodic The chain has no periodic structure. A chain is periodic if some states can only be revisited at regular intervals. ⚠️ Pitfall: Bipartite graphs have period 2 — you alternate sides. At odd times you're on one side, even times on the other. graph LR L1 --> R1 L1 --> R2 R1 --> L1 R1 --> L2 R2 --> L2 L2 --> R1 If you start on the left, at every even time you're on the left, every odd time on the right. Starting state matters! Fix: Add self-loops (P(i, i) > 0 for all i). Even a tiny self-loop probability destroys periodicity. The Ergodic Theorem Theorem: If a Markov chain is ergodic (irreducible + aperiodic), then: There exists a unique stationary distribution π For any starting distribution μ₀, μ₀ · Pᵏ → π as k → ∞ Every row of Pᵏ converges to π Sufficient condition (easy to check): If P(i, j) > 0 for ALL i, j (every entry positive), then the chain is ergodic. When Can We Compute π? Case π P is symmetric: P(i,j) = P(j,i) π is uniform : π(i) = 1/N for all i P is reversible: π(i)P(i,j) = π(j)P(j,i) Can solve for π using detailed balance General No closed form — compute via Pᵏ for large k 6. PageRank — Motivation Problem: The web is a directed graph (vertices = pages, edges = hyperlinks). When someone searches for "Markov chains," many pages match. How do you rank them by importance ? Idea 1: Count incoming links π(x) = |in(x)| (in-degree) Problem: A link from CNN is worth more than a link from some random page. All links shouldn't count equally. Idea 2: Scale by number of outgoing links π(x) = Σ_{y ∈ in(x)} 1/|out(y)| If page y has 1000 links, each one is worth 1/1000. If it has 5 links, each is worth 1/5. Problem: A link from CNN should be worth more than a link from my kid's homepage, even if they have the same number of outgoing links. The importance of the source matters. Idea 3: Weight by source importance (recursive!) $$\pi(x) = \sum_{y \in in(x)} \frac{\pi(y)}{|out(y)|}$$ A citation from page y is worth π(y)/|out(y)| — proportional to y's importance, divided among its outgoing links. This is a recursive definition — π appears on both sides. Is it well-defined? Is there a unique solution? 💡 Intuition: This is exactly the equation πP = π for a random walk on the webgraph! PageRank = stationary distribution. 7. The Random Surfer Model Imagine a "random surfer" who: Starts at any webpage At each step, follows a random outgoing hyperlink This defines a Markov chain with transition matrix: $$P(y, x) = \begin{cases} 1/|out(y)| & \text{if } y \to x \text{ is a hyperlink} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ The stationary distribution of this chain satisfies exactly the PageRank equation from above! But there are problems: The webgraph has multiple SCCs → not irreducible Parts may be bipartite → periodic Some pages are sink nodes (no outgoing links) → transition undefined 8. Fixing the Problems — The Damping Parameter To ensure ergodicity, we modify the random walk with a damping parameter α ∈ (0, 1): At each step: With probability α : follow a random outgoing hyperlink With probability 1 - α : jump to a random page uniformly from ALL pages This is the random surfer with a "random button." Google reportedly uses α ≈ 0.85 . The Modified Transition Matrix For N total webpages: $$P'(y, x) = \begin{cases} \alpha \cdot \frac{1}{|out(y)|} + (1-\alpha) \cdot \frac{1}{N} & \text{if } y \to x \in E \\ (1-\alpha) \cdot \frac{1}{N} & \text{if } y \to x \notin E \end{cases}$$ Since α < 1, every entry P'(y, x) > 0 . The graph is fully connected → irreducible AND aperiodic → ergodic . Therefore: a unique π exists, and it's the PageRank vector. 9. Handling Sink Nodes A sink node x has no outgoing links: |out(x)| = 0. The transition matrix is undefined for row x. Several fixes: Approach How Downside Self-loop With prob α, stay at x Artificially boosts x's rank Remove sinks Recursively delete Shrinks graph, some pages unranked Random jump With prob 1, jump to random page (set α=0 for sinks) Most natural; apparently what Google does With the random jump approach: for sink node x, set P'(x, j) = 1/N for all j. 10. Computing PageRank in Practice Method: Power iteration — repeatedly multiply by P. FindPageRank(P', μ₀): Input: Transition matrix P', initial distribution μ₀ Output: Approximate stationary distribution π μ = μ₀ repeat until convergence: μ_new = μ · P' if ||μ_new - μ|| < ε: return μ_new μ = μ_new Key considerations: P' is N × N where N = number of webpages (billions!). O(N²) is too expensive. But P' is sparse — the original webgraph has O(N) edges (constant out-degree on average) Matrix-vector multiplication μ · P' takes O(m) time where m = number of edges Convergence is fast because the random jump mixes things quickly In practice, use last week's π as the starting μ₀ for faster convergence 11. Putting It All Together graph TD A["Web Graph G
(pages + hyperlinks)"] --> B["Build transition matrix P
P(y,x) = 1/|out(y)|"] B --> C["Add damping: P' = αP + (1-α)·1/N
(handles SCCs, periodicity, sinks)"] C --> D["Power iteration: μ·P'^k → π"] D --> E["π = PageRank vector
π(x) = importance of page x"] Component Role Random walk on webgraph Natural importance measure Damping parameter α Ensures ergodicity (unique π) Stationary distribution π = PageRank (importance) πP = π Eigenvector equation Power iteration Efficient computation 12. Summary Concept Key Point Markov chain Random walk defined by stochastic matrix P Pᵏ(i,j) Probability of i → j in k steps Stationary distribution π such that πP = π; left eigenvector with eigenvalue 1 Ergodic Irreducible (1 SCC) + aperiodic (self-loops); guarantees unique π PageRank π(x) = Σ π(y)/ Random surfer With prob α follow link, prob 1-α jump randomly α (damping) ≈ 0.85; ensures full connectivity; balances fidelity vs convergence Sink nodes Set α = 0 (always random jump) Computing π Power iteration μ · P'^k; O(m) per iteration 🎯 Exam Tip: Know the connection between the three perspectives: (1) citation counting, (2) random walks/Markov chains, (3) eigenvectors. They all give the same equation. ⚠️ Common Pitfall: The webgraph is NOT ergodic by itself (multiple SCCs, sinks, possible bipartiteness). The damping parameter is essential — without it, PageRank is not well-defined.

title: 📝 Graphs Cheat Sheet — CS 6515
text: 📝 Graphs Cheat Sheet — CS 6515 Algorithms at a Glance Algorithm Input Output Runtime Key Idea BFS G, source s dist[], prev[] O(n+m) Queue; shortest paths (unweighted) Dijkstra's G, s, w(e)>0 dist[], prev[] O((V+E)log V) Min-heap BFS; positive weights only DFS G pre[], post[], ccnum[] O(n+m) Recursion; foundation for everything Topo Sort DAG ordered vertices O(n+m) DFS, sort by decreasing post number SCC Directed G SCC labels O(n+m) DFS on G^R, then DFS on G 2-SAT 2-CNF formula assignment or NO O(n+m) Implication graph + SCC Kruskal's Undirected G, weights MST O(E log V) Sort edges; Union-Find Prim's Undirected G, weights MST O(E log V) Grow tree; min-heap Key Lemmas & Theorems Cycle Detection G has a cycle ⟺ DFS tree has a back edge SCC Source Lemma Vertex with highest post number (in DFS on G^R) is in a source SCC of G^R = sink SCC of G 2-SAT Lemma f is satisfiable ⟺ ∀i, xᵢ and x̄ᵢ are in different SCCs Cut Property (MST) A minimum-weight edge crossing any cut (S, S̄) is in some MST. Proof idea: If MST T doesn't contain e*, add e* (creates cycle), remove another cut edge e'. w(T') ≤ w(T). Ergodic Theorem (Markov Chains) Irreducible + aperiodic ⟹ unique stationary distribution π, and Pᵏ → π regardless of start. Edge Types in DFS (Directed Graphs) Type Direction post(z) vs post(w) Tree Parent → child post(z) > post(w) Back Descendant → ancestor post(z) < post(w) ⚠️ Forward Ancestor → descendant post(z) > post(w) Cross No ancestor relation post(z) > post(w) Only back edges have post(z) < post(w). Everything else: post(z) > post(w). SCC Algorithm — Quick Steps Build G^R (reverse edges) DFS(G^R) → get post numbers Order vertices by decreasing post number DFS(G) in that order → each Explore = one SCC 2-SAT — Quick Steps Build implication graph: clause (α ∨ β) → edges ᾱ→β and β̄→α Run SCC algorithm If any xᵢ and x̄ᵢ in same SCC → unsatisfiable Assign: sink SCC = TRUE, its complement (source) = FALSE, repeat MST — Quick Reminders Kruskal's: Sort edges, add lightest if no cycle (Union-Find) Prim's: Grow one tree, add lightest cut edge (min-heap) Both correct via Cut Property Trees: n-1 edges, connected, acyclic (any 2 ⟹ 3rd) PageRank — Quick Formula $$\pi(x) = \sum_{y \in in(x)} \frac{\pi(y)}{|out(y)|}$$ Equivalent to πP = π (stationary distribution) Damping: P' = αP + (1-α)·(1/N)· J , with α ≈ 0.85 Sink nodes: random jump (α = 0) Compute via power iteration: μ · P'^k → π ⚠️ Common Pitfalls Pitfall Why It's Wrong Using Dijkstra's with negative weights Can give wrong shortest paths; use Bellman-Ford Topological sort on a cyclic graph Impossible — check for back edges first Confusing 2-SAT implication direction (α ∨ β) gives ᾱ→β, NOT α→β Assuming MST is unique Multiple MSTs possible if edges have equal weights (total weight is unique) Assuming webgraph is ergodic It's not — damping parameter is essential Forgetting Markov chains need stochastic matrix Every row must sum to 1 🎯 Exam Tips DFS is the Swiss Army knife — SCCs, topo sort, cycle detection all build on it Cut Property proof — high probability exam question. Know the swap argument. 2-SAT construction — practice converting clauses to implication edges quickly SCC order matters — DFS on G^R first, then G. Not the other way around. Runtimes are all O(n+m) for graph decomposition algorithms (BFS, DFS, SCC, 2-SAT, topo sort). Only MST requires sorting: O(E log V). PageRank = stationary distribution — know the three equivalent views (citation, random walk, eigenvector)

title: Usable Black Boxes for Graphs
text: Usable Black Boxes for Graphs Category : Staff Use Only > Supplemental Material Date : 2026-06-15 17:48 Link : https://edstem.org/us/courses/98593/discussion/8129088 Pinned : True | Votes : 5 | Views : 1850 Post For the graphs section, you must use the algorithms presented in the course materials to help you solve presented problems. That is, solutions in this section must use one (or a combo) of the black boxes to solve the presented problem. Providing full implementation details of one of these black boxes, and adding in a twist or in-line tracking will be treated as a modification.Many graphs algorithms exist beyond what is covered in this course; however, only those explicitly mentioned here may be used. The use of extra-curricular algorithms will result in penalties, including for variations of these algorithms outside of the lectures, book, and this post.Wikipedia entries are provided for supplemental reading, such as history and discovery of these algorithms. Where differences exist, this post represents the version used in this course.All runtimes below are presented assuming n = |vertices| and m = |edges| .All outputs below are produced as n-sized lists, containing an entry for each vertex in the graph, and are able to be indexed by vertex in O(1) time to read its contents, unless otherwise noted.The following black boxes are available for use during the remainder of the course: Depth-First Search (DFS) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth-first_search ]- Input: A simple graph in adjacency list format A starting vertex This is optional. If not provided, DFS will start from an arbitrary location. This is accomplished through adjacency list ordering, which we assume takes place when you provide a starting vertex. Internal (not accessible after run) : visited[] - A list containing whether the indexed vertex was touched by DFS. All entries of this list will always be set to true when DFS completes. This is populated by Explore, an internal subroutine of DFS. Output: ccnum[] - A list containing the connected component number of the indexed vertex. Vertices reachable from the starting vertex will have a connected component number of 1 . prev[] - A list containing the parent vertex of the indexed vertex, which can be used to create a path from the starting vertex to any reachable vertex. Unreachable vertices and the starting vertex have a parent of nil . pre[] - A list containing the pre-visit number for the indexed vertex. post[] - A list containing the post-visit number for the indexed vertex. Runtime: O(n + m) Implementation details: DPV pp. 83-91 GR1.3, GR1.6 Common uses: Finding connected components on a graph Finding a cycle in a graph Producing a path from starting vertex to a reachable vertex Topological Sort (see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_sorting )- Input: A simple, directed, acyclic graph in adjacency list format Output: order[] - A list of vertices, sorted in topological ordering from source to sink. Note: This output is indexed numerically rather than by vertex. All outputs from the run of Depth-First Search (DFS) are also available to you. Runtime: O(n + m) Implementation details: DPV pp. 89-91 GR1.10 Common uses: Finding the topological sorting in a DAG Strongly Connected Components (SCC) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strongly_connected_component ]- Input: A simple, directed graph in adjacency list format Output: G_SCC = (V_SCC, E_SCC) - The strongly connected components metagraph, provided in adjacency list format. By construction, the metagraph is a DAG with vertices sorted from sink to source This ordering is known as reverse topological ordering. All outputs from the final run of Depth-First Search (DFS) are also available to you. This data is used to connect entities in the metagraph to the original input graph. For example, the first vertex in V_SCC represents all vertices with ccnum[v] = 1 from the DFS outputs from the original input graph. Runtime: O(n + m) Implementation details: DPV pp. 91-95 GR1.21 Common uses: Finding strongly connected components on a graph Particularly useful for finding source and sink SCCs Breadth-First Search (BFS) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadth-first_search ]- Input: A simple graph in adjacency list format A starting vertex Output: dist[] - A list containing the unweighted distance from the starting vertex to the indexed vertex for all vertices in the graph. Unreachable vertices have a distance of inf . prev[] - A list containing the parent vertex of the indexed vertex, which can be used to create a path from the starting vertex to any reachable vertex. Unreachable vertices and the starting vertex have a parent of nil . Runtime: O(n + m) Implementation details: DPV pp. 105-106 GR1.24 Common uses: Reachability analysis Unweighted shortest path determination Producing a path from starting vertex to a reachable vertex Dijkstra's (see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijkstra%27s_algorithm )- Input: A simple graph in adjacency list format A starting vertex A list of non-negative edge weights Output: dist[] - A list containing the weighted distance from the starting vertex to the indexed vertex for all vertices in the graph. Unreachable vertices have a distance of inf . prev[] - A list containing the parent vertex of the indexed vertex, which can be used to create a path from the starting vertex to any reachable vertex. Unreachable vertices and the starting vertex have a parent of nil . Runtime: O((n + m) log n) Implementation details: DPV pp. 109-115 GR1.24 Common uses: Reachability analysis Weighted shortest path determination Producing a path from starting vertex to a reachable vertex Bellman-Ford (BF) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellman%E2%80%93Ford_algorithm ]- Input: A simple graph in adjacency list format A starting vertex A list of edge weights Output: dist[] - A list containing the weighted distance from the starting vertex to the indexed vertex for all vertices in the graph. Unreachable vertices have a distance of inf . Values are based on the n-1 th iteration. prev[] - A list containing the parent vertex of the indexed vertex, which can be used to create a path from the starting vertex to any reachable vertex. Unreachable vertices and the starting vertex have a parent of nil . iter[][] - A 2-dimensional list containing the first indexed iteration's shortest path from the starting vertex to the second indexed vertex. For example, iter[3][v] contains the distance from the starting vertex to v at the end of the 3rd iteration. This table contains iterations 0 through n . Runtime: O(nm) Implementation details: DPV pp. 115-119 DP3.6 Common uses: Reachability analysis Weighted shortest path determination Negative cycle detection Producing a path from starting vertex to a reachable vertex Floyd-Warshall (FW) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floyd%E2%80%93Warshall_algorithm ]- Input: A simple graph in adjacency list format A list of edge weights Output: dist[][] - A 2-dimensional list containing the weighted distance from the first indexed vertex to the second indexed vertex. For example, dist[u][v] would contain the shortest path from vertex u to vertex v . Unreachable vertex pairs have a distance of inf . Values are based on the nth iteration. iter[][][] - A 3-dimensional list containing the first indexed iteration's shortest path from the second indexed vertex to the third indexed vertex. For example, iter[3][u][v] contains the distance from u to v at the end of the 3rd iteration. This table contains iterations 0 through n . Runtime: O(n^3) Implementation details: DPV pp. 172-173 DP3.17 Common uses: Reachability analysis Weighted shortest path determination Negative cycle detection Kruskal's (see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kruskal%27s_algorithm )- Input: A simple, connected, undirected graph in adjacency list format A list of edge weights Output: edges[] - A list of n-1 edges that represent a minimum spanning tree for the input graph. Runtime: O(m log n) Implementation details: DPV pp. 128-137 GR3.6 Common uses: Producing a minimum spanning tree Prim's (see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prim%27s_algorithm )- Input: A simple, connected, undirected graph in adjacency list format A list of edge weights Output: prev[] - A list containing the parent vertex of the indexed vertex, which represent the connecting edges of a minimum spanning tree for the input graph. The starting vertex is chosen arbitrarily and has a parent of nil . Runtime: O(m log n) Implementation details: DPV pp. 137-139 GR3.15 Common uses: Producing a minimum spanning tree Ford-Fulkerson (FF) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford%E2%80%93Fulkerson_algorithm ]- Input: A simple, connected, directed graph in adjacency list format A list of positive, integer edge capacities A starting source vertex A terminating sink vertex Output: flow[] - A list of edges representing the amount capacity used per each indexed edge such that the flow is maximized from the starting vertex to the terminating vertex. C - The value of the maximum flow from the starting vertex to the terminating vertex. Runtime: O(mC) Implementation details: DPV pp. 198-204 MF1.14 Common uses: Finding max flows on a graph Edmonds-Karp (EK) [see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonds%E2%80%93Karp_algorithm ]- Input: A simple, connected, directed graph in adjacency list format A list of positive edge capacities A starting source vertex A terminating sink vertex Output: flow[] - A list of edges representing the amount capacity used per each indexed edge such that the flow is maximized from the starting vertex to the terminating vertex. C - The value of the maximum flow from the starting vertex to the terminating vertex. Runtime: O(nm^2) Implementation details: DPV pp. 198-204 MF4.3 Common uses: Finding max flows on a graph 2-SAT (see also: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2-satisfiability )- Input: A Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form such that each clause contains at most 2 literals. This formula is backed by a list of n variables, representing at most 2n literals and m clauses. Output: assignments[] - A list indexable by the variables that back the original input formula containing whether that variable is set to true or false . If the input is not satisfiable, this will instead return "NO" All outputs from the Strongly Connected Components (SCC) run are also available to you. Runtime: O(n + m) Implementation details: DPV p. 101 GR2 Common uses: Example of how graphs algorithms can be used to solve a problem that starts in a non-graphs domain Converting a graph representation into a Boolean formula to determine satisfiability of the task at hand Responses (9) Comment by User 821283 on 2026-06-16 11:40 (Votes: 1) Thanks for posting this! I have two questions: Will the name of each algorithm provided in exam 2? Or, do we need to memorize the name? For max flow algorithms, output flow[] is indexed by edge. Does that mean edges can be indexed as 1, 2, ... m, and looking up an edge takes O(1) time (similar to the indexing of vertices)? (Though I'll actually spell out the whole name "Dijkstra" on submitted materials, as sadly there is no (DJ) in parens as an abbreviation) Comment by User 658839 on 2026-06-18 02:45 (Votes: 0) Will we be tested on performing these algorithms by hand? Or focus is on just using them? Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-18 08:23 (Votes: 0) See the intro to #191. Comment by User 821283 on 2026-06-19 09:26 (Votes: 1) The max flow algorithms require the input to be a "connected directed graph" (but not necessarily strongly connected), and I am wondering what does that mean. title: Graph Theory Guidance
text: Graph Theory Guidance Category : Staff Use Only > Supplemental Material Date : 2026-06-15 17:47 Link : https://edstem.org/us/courses/98593/discussion/8129087 Pinned : True | Votes : 3 | Views : 1437 Post Below you will find information on how you should approach solving Graph Theory problems in this class. Feel free to ask questions about writing a Graph Theory solution in this thread. Context A graph theory problem is a form of reduction . You are given some problem to solve, and the challenge is to solve that problem by using one of the graph algorithms we study this semester. In other words, you reduce your problem to a graph problem such that a known algorithm can solve it for you. The known algorithms (#192) are treated as a black-box - you are not allowed to change / modify them in any way. You can (and often will) modify the original problem input in some way or create a graph which represents the input - this becomes the input to the black-box. You then use the outputs from the black-box (possibly with modification) to output a solution to the original problem. Rules NO PSEUDOCODE - YOU WILL LOSE A LOT OF POINTS You may only use known black box algorithms (#192). You must use one or more black box algorithms (#192) to solve problems. You must not modify any black box algorithms (#192). Re-creating a black box with modifications is the same thing. All graphs are in adjacency list format (see below) You can assume you always have n and m for purposes of runtime analysis, where n represents the number of vertices |V| and m represents the number of edges |E|. #192 isn't exactly relevant here, but it's worth another link. See #8 for common course runtimes, including operations performed to graphs. Required Parts of a Graph Theory Solution (a) Algorithm Describe "how" to solve the problem in words (narrative/paragraph form) Bulleted steps are fine, but pseudocode/code is not allowed "Pseudocode" includes line-by-line restatement of code as words. If you find yourself using a lot of nested bullets, you might be erring on the side of line-by-line conversion of code into words, which is not a narrative. Describe what modifications are performed to the input , if any Detail the black box algorithm(s) being used What is passed in as input What is being used from its output Describe what modifications are performed to the output , if any Repeat as needed for any other black boxes Detail the final return for the problem's solution (b) Justification of Correctness Describe "why" your algorithm solves the problem, in words (narrative). This is not a formal inductive proof; informal justification is ok. Explain how your problem is solved by the black boxes used Explain how changing the inputs and/or outputs gets what you want (c) Runtime Analysis Analyze all steps of the algorithm in Big-O notation . Always, always in this course - worst case Big-O. Can explain/analyze in words and assert known black-box runtimes without further justification. Must include run time analysis for any pre/post processing See #8 for common runtimes when dealing with graphs. Provide an overall final runtime in (you guessed it) Big-O notation, fully simplified. If the problem specifies a target runtime, you must meet that for full credit. If we do not specify a runtime, faster (and correct) in Big O notation are worth more credit. While we work with worse-case runtimes, we also work with tightest-bound runtimes. That is, even though the worst case for an O(n+m) operation occurs when m= n^2, it is incorrect to state O(n^2) for such an operation unless we know something about the graph (e.g., it is a clique). O(n+m) is the tightest worse-case bound on such an operation Similarly, if we know the graph is a tree, then m = n-1 and O(n+m) operations collapse to O(n). When conveying the well-known runtimes of usable black boxes, you are not required to simplify it, even if the graph's constraints would allow for it. Graph Representation Graphs in this class, unless stated otherwise : Are simple graphs (no multi-edges or self-loops) Are always given in adjacency list format (see DPV 3.1.1) An array of vertices that are pointers to linked lists of adjacent vertices, such that each element in the list represents an edge to another vertex. Vertices are assumed to be labeled in such a way where they can be found by indexing into the array. Can be connected or disconnected, undirected or directed, sparse or dense If unstated by the problem, you should assume any of these could be true Are connected and undirected when working with MSTs Are connected and directed when working with flow networks When working with graphs, there are a number of common actions that can be presented without needing to go into details. Some examples as follows: Reversing a graph: "Reverse the edges in the graph". Copying a graph: "Create a copy of G and call it GCopy". Creating subgraphs: "Create a copy of G called GEven that only keeps edges with even numbered weights". "Create a copy of G called GK that only keeps vertices with a degree > k". "Create a residual graph of G called Grs that uses the flows from our run of EK". Unless the task can't directly be completed in this runtime, each of these are assumed to be O(n + m) operations. Please ask questions regarding the expectations for Graph Theory problems in this thread. Responses (7) Comment by User 821283 on 2026-06-18 14:29 (Votes: 2) Is that ok if my algorithm include 1 (or more) black box algorithm, but has also other non-trivial steps that traverse the graph? As an example, the 2nd part of the algorithm below is not a black box, but the 1st part is. Is that acceptable? Examples for 3.16 (minimum number of semesters necessary to complete the curriculum) Run topological sort on the graph. Under topological order, find the first vertex with incoming edges, remove all vertices before that from the graph, and add one semester. Repeat this step until graph is empty. Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-18 23:49 (Votes: 2) Yes, it's common that, as part of your solutions, there may be pre-processing or post-processing work that takes place around the black box usage. This could be creating subgraphs, modifying graphs, performing graph traversal, doing calculations, etc. Comment by User 813950 on 2026-06-19 08:41 (Votes: 0) I see that it says its graded; only this homework is graded? Comment by User 135758 on 2026-06-19 09:01 (Votes: 0) Is this for Homework 5? "Graded" generally means "marked for feedback". The weighting of those markings is unchanged from the syllabus. Comment by User 813950 on 2026-06-19 09:38 (Votes: 0) yes; sorry I got confused when i saw highlighted word graded. Thanks Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-19 09:43 (Votes: 0) Yes. If you make a submission, the graders grade and so it goes. Comment by User 585876 on 2026-06-19 23:11 (Votes: 0) Just to clarify wording: Similarly, if we know the graph is a tree, then m = n-1 and O(n+m) operations collapse to O(n). Is this saying that because we know that the graph is a tree, the tightest bound is O(n) or that even though we know it's a tree, the tightest bound should be reported as O(n+m) because that's what the operation runtime is Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-20 01:31 (Votes: 2) When it is a tree, we know that we have n vertices and exactly n-1 edges. If the input you are given is a tree, then O(n) and O(n + m) are the same, given that m has an exact definition, which enables simplification to O(n) . If the input you are given is not specified to be a tree (but we know it's connected), and you produce a tree (say with Kruskal's), then we have that m >= n-1 and O(n) becomes a tighter bound when performing work on the produced tree. Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-06-20 15:02 (Votes: 0) So just to clarify: Operate on the connected graph to produce your tree: O(m) but NOT O(n) (since graph is connected, m >= n-1) Operate on the produced tree: O(n) or O(m) (equivalent, because m = n - 1 for tree) Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-20 23:50 (Votes: 0) Operate on the produced tree: O(n) or O(m) (equivalent, because m = n - 1 for tree) For a produced tree - that is one like my example above, which could have come from a complete graph where m ~ n^2 - we have no assurance that m and n are equivalent. But we do know properties of a tree allow us to provide a tighter bound, if we go on to work on that tree. For a given tree - that is, the input to the problem is told to be a tree - then we do know they're equivalent, again based on a property of trees. Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-06-21 02:07 (Votes: 0) I think I was a bit loose on my definitions here, so let me clarify once more: Operate on a tree (m = n - 1 for tree): O(n+m) = O(n) = O(m). Operate on a generic connected graph (n-1 <= m <= n(n-1) for directed graph). So m = O(n^2) and n = O(m). Hence: O(n+m) = O(O(m) + m) = O(m). And also, O(n+m) = O(n + O(n^2)) = O(n^2). Comment by User 802900 on 2026-06-20 15:06 (Votes: 0) Why is the size of the adjacency list O(|E|) if each edge is represented twice? I would assume O(2|E|). Is this like runtime where we remove constant factors? Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-06-20 16:55 (Votes: 1) That's right, constant factors are ignored in Big-O notation. Just like how O(2n) == O(n). Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-06-20 16:56 (Votes: 0) I was looking at this example, and I was wondering if the task "find the vertex with largest degree" would have runtime: O(n) - if the metadata "number of edges" is stored on each vertex OR O(n+m) - if you need to count the number of edges manually But I'm not sure what is stored as metadata on each vertex? Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-20 23:55 (Votes: 1) The adjacency list, like our normal lists, do not store any metadata. So, no shortcuts on length finding. You'll see through the way the book and lectures talk, and when we get to the programming homework, that "metadata" such as lengths, weights, colors are actually separate structures entirely. The graph theory black boxes post in #192 also treats them this way. Given that, if you need to find the vertex with the largest degree, you'll need to count the number of neighbors for every vertex in the adjacency list, and you'd end up at O(n + m) overall. Comment by User 1282049 on 2026-06-21 01:42 (Votes: 0) Thank you Comment by User 1135584 on 2026-06-20 21:29 (Votes: 1) The lectures spend a lot of time on the proofs of correctness for these black box algorithms. The ed posts and homeworks make it seem like it will be important for us to know the inputs and outputs and generally what these blackboxes are doing so we can use them to solve graph problems. How important is it to study/memorize the proofs from the lectures? Comment by User 137215 on 2026-06-21 00:00 (Votes: 0) How important is it to study/memorize the proofs from the lectures? The information Dr. Vigoda covers in the lectures for the proofs of correctness will prove quite insightful for student justification of correctness, just at "the next level". While you do not need to rederive the correctness of the black box, your solution will depend on some or all of its behavior, which you will have exploited in some way to solve the problem. That would be a great thing to include for why your algorithm works. And then of course, there's the entire portion of the course that isn't free response questions... For example: we can remove an edge from G in O(1) time but creating a copy without the same edge could cost us O(n+m).
